articles.title_orig: World-famous science educator Bill Nye believes in Titans: ‘You're going to change the world’
articles.title_zh: World-famous science educator Bill Nye believes in Titans: ‘You're going to change the world’
articles.content_orig:
When the first notes of the “Bill Nye the Science Guy” theme song began echoing through the Titan Student Union Portola Pavilion, students didn’t miss a beat. They sang along to the popular chorus — “Bill, Bill, Bill, Bill, Bill, Bill” — as the world-famous scientist and educator took the stage for the “Beyond the Conversation” series at Cal State Fullerton.
Hosted by Associated Students Inc., the signature series invites notable speakers to campus to share their stories and spark dialogue among students. Bill Nye, who spoke to the Titan community on Oct. 7, joins a star-studded lineup of previous “Beyond the Conversation” speakers, including Olympic swimmer Michael Phelps , Oscar winner Ke Huy Quan , and Emmy and Grammy Award-winning actress Cynthia Erivo .
As the co-creator and host of the Emmy Award-winning ’90s television series “Bill Nye the Science Guy,” Nye has emerged not only as an entertaining educator but also as an influential advocate for science and facts in an era of misinformation.
His lifelong commitment to advocacy has earned him various honors, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, inclusion in the Time 100 Health list, a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, and a Lifetime Achievement Award from the Children’s & Family Emmy Awards.
Nye has made science and engineering education entertaining and accessible for generations of viewers. He shared his story with Cal State Fullerton students and imparted a few pieces of advice and encouragement to help them on their academic journey.
Getting a college education gives you a way of looking at the world that is essentially priceless. You are going to go out there and dare I say it, change the world.  — Bill Nye
“You guys are going to graduate from Cal State Fullerton with this degree, and it will be worth more the day after you graduate than the day you graduate. I guarantee you,” Nye said.
“Getting a college education gives you a way of looking at the world that is essentially priceless. You are going to go out there and dare I say it, change the world.”
With the rapid expansion of social media and artificial intelligence, Nye acknowledged that students have access to a wealth of information about science, the environment and sustainability. He said the key to consuming and identifying reliable information is critical thinking.
As a scientist who has spent his career asking questions and investigating the wonders of the world, Nye said critical thinking isn’t about questioning everything and assuming everything is wrong. It’s about evaluating evidence before deciding if a claim is true.
“What we want everybody to embrace is what is nowadays called critical thinking. It used to be called logic or logical reasoning, but we want everybody to be in the habit of evaluating evidence,” Nye explained.
For students who are preparing to launch their careers, Nye said it’s important to lead with passion and curiosity and to take that first step.
“My advice is to just get started. You don’t know where it’s going to lead, but find something you want to do or something that you wouldn’t mind doing, and get started,” Nye said.
“The thing that goes wrong is when you have so many things to do, you just can’t get going. Just get started. You’re going to change the world.”
Nye was interviewed by Nathan Hoang, a fourth-year business administration student and student programmer for ASI’s student programs and engagement team.
“Events like ‘Beyond the Conversation’ inspire students to see themselves in these figures and empower them to believe maybe they can one day be on that stage as well,” Hoang said. “What stood out to me about Bill’s interview was how he kept the conversation fun, but still didn’t shy away from pointing out our responsibilities as young adults and the potential we have to shape the future.”

Growers of giant pumpkins and their colossal gourds will gather on Monday in Northern California for an annual weighing competition, vying for the top award and a chance to challenge a world record set just last week in England .
At least 30 growers have registered for the 53rd World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off in Half Moon Bay, south of San Francisco , according to event spokesman Ronan Fowler.
Among those competing is four-time champion Travis Gienger, a horticulture teacher from Minnesota whose winning run ended last year when he couldn't enter because his pumpkin split while still growing.
Gienger, who navigated freezing temperatures this growing season, produced a pumpkin with a circumference large enough to make it a potential world-record contender, Fowler said.
Fowler mentioned last week that Gienger and his father intended to alternate behind the wheel during a 30-hour drive over the weekend to deliver the small-car-sized pumpkin to California.
Ian Paton of Lymington, on the southern coast of England, set the existing world record with a giant squash weighing 2,857 pounds (1,296 kilograms). That figure exceeds the combined weight of two-and-a-half concert grand pianos.
Paton raises his massive gourds in a greenhouse, while Gienger cultivates his entries in a backyard pumpkin patch in Anoka, a city along the Mississippi River north of Minneapolis , Fowler noted.
"The fact that Travis can weather the elements, like 30-degree weather, and still grow this massive pumpkin is pretty unbelievable," the spokesman said.
Brandon Dawson, a resident of Santa Rosa , California, who won first place last year with a massive pumpkin weighing 2,346 pounds (1,064 kilograms), will also compete in the contest.
The winning grower this year will earn $9 for each pound of pumpkin and will have their giant gourd displayed during a parade through Half Moon Bay over the weekend. Should the winning entry surpass the world record, the competitor will receive an additional $30,000 prize.
Monday's proceedings, which mark the beginning of the city's autumn celebrations, will also feature a special appearance by pumpkin carver Mike Valladao.
However, these giant gourds are grown for size rather than flavor, so no oversized pumpkin pies will be served at the end of the event.

articles.title_zh: Sixth person who had measles has died in Pennsylvania, local coroner says
articles.content_orig:

A sixth person infected with measles has died in Pennsylvania after the worst outbreak of the virus in the state in over 35 years.
The 39-year-old woman had underlying health conditions and had previously been treated for measles, the Franklin County Coroner’s Office said Monday.
“This is the first death in Franklin County in many years with a patient with a recent history of a measles diagnosis and meets the definition set forth by the Pennsylvania Department of Health for a measles-associated death ,” the coroner’s office wrote in a statement, shared to Facebook.
The office said it would not release any additional details about the case.
Measles is spreading across Pennsylvania and in other parts of the U.S. The state’s Department of Health reported 1,136 cases since the start of the year and 157 in the last week alone.
Pennsylvania’s measles tracker showed five deaths Monday but a note explained the next update would be Wednesday due to the Columbus Day and Indigenous Peoples’ Day holiday.
The state’s Health Department told The Independent it is aware of the death reported by the Franklin County coroner.
“Our team has reached out to the coroner’s office and is conducting a thorough review of the reported death. We will update the public after our investigation is finished,” Press Secretary Neil Ruhland said via email.
As part of the investigation, the department will rely on its definition for a measles-associated death, he noted.
The department defines a measles-associated death as one that occurs within 30 days of the start of symptoms of infection, with clinical evidence of an infection, a positive lab test for measles and no other unrelated causes.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention only reports two deaths from measles in Pennsylvania.
There have been no updates to the federal death count since late September. A note above the data states the total is subject to change as more information becomes available and “relevant reviews are completed.”
Pennsylvania’s first measles death was reported in late August. It was also the first measles death of the year in the U.S.
Health Sec. Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro have traded shots at each other on social media over the numbers.
Shapiro blasted what he called the Trump administration’s “incompetence” in responding to the virus and Kennedy initially claimed that Pennsylvania’s measles deaths were “ fabricated.”
The CDC previously told The Independent that the agency had "mounted an aggressive response to measles outbreaks across the country.”
HHS did not immediately respond to The Independent’s request for comment on the death count.
There are 4,080 confirmed measles cases this year in the District of Columbia and 46 states. There have also been 42 new outbreaks in 2026.
Last year, there were 2,289 confirmed measles cases. Some outbreaks from 2025 continued into the beginning of this year, including in Utah and South Carolina.
Measles is a highly contagious virus that can cause life-threatening brain-swelling and high fever, especially in those who have not received two doses of the MMR vaccine.
Vaccination provides lifelong protection against infection and severe illness. But rising vaccine hesitancy and misinformation has led cases to reach the worst levels since the 1990s, doctors previously told The Independent .
The U.S. is now at risk of losing its long-held elimination status , medical experts say , because there has been continuous spread of measles for more than a year.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he's "looking at" firing Kimberly Guilfoyle: "We're not happy"
articles.title_zh: Trump says he's "looking at" firing Kimberly Guilfoyle: "We're not happy"
articles.content_orig:
Washington — President Trump said he and his administration are "looking at" firing Kimberly Guilfoyle from her position as U.S. ambassador to Greece, after an associate of Guilfoyle's alleged she asked him to wire $100,000 to pay her American Express bill in exchange for her help with the Trump administration ahead of her Senate confirmation hearing.
"Well, we're looking at it," the president told reporters on his way to Ohio when asked if he's considering firing Guilfoyle. "We're not happy."
Businessman Eric Deters told CBS News last week he has "no doubt it was pay-to-play" when Guilfoyle asked for funds. Deters also provided CBS News with screenshots of his texts with Guilfoyle, including one message in which she appeared to ask him to wire money. Deters said he never gave her the money.
"Unfortunately for Kimberly Guilfoyle, at that time, at that moment in time, I didn't have $100,000 to spare to give to Kimberly Guilfoyle, or I actually would have been a dumbass enough to do it."
White House officials were told that the text messages between Guilfoyle and Deters were authentic, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News last week. Some Trump aides expressed displeasure about Guilfoyle's actions, they said.
Guilfoyle's lawyer disputed the authenticity of the texts to The Wall Street Journal, which was first to report on them.
Guilfoyle, nominated by Mr. Trump to serve as his top envoy to Greece, is the ex-fiancée of Donald Trump Jr. Her confirmation hearing was held in July 2025, and she was confirmed in September of that year.
She was highly visible during Secretary of State Marco Rubio's visit to Greece last week. At the time, Rubio did not respond to questions about Deter's allegations, telling reporters: "I'm not going to comment on a story that literally posted a few hours ago."

articles.title_zh: The University of California is a world leader, according to this new global ranking
articles.content_orig:
At home and abroad, the UC system is unrivaled. That’s according to new rankings from Times Higher Education, a U.K.-based publication.
The World University 2027 rankings identified UC’s nine undergraduate campuses as among the best 50 public universities in the United States. Six UC campuses are among the nation’s top 40, private or public, and all nine undergraduate campuses are among the top 20% of all universities around the world.
The rankings evaluate five main factors — teaching, research, the economic footprint of that research, and international staff, students and research collaborations — across a pool of 2,297 universities in 118 countries and territories.
*The World University rankings group universities into bands after the top 200.
The University of California is at the very top of a variety of rankings. Those include rankings of student outcomes ( Forbes ), global reputation ( U.S. News ), universities that produce startups ( Pitchbook ) and the U.S. News Best Colleges rankings , which have named a University of California campus the nation’s top public every year since its 1999 edition.
The Times Higher Education World University ranking originated in 2004. It’s named UC Berkeley the top public university in the U.S. for 11 of the past 12 years.

The No. 1 ranking highlights UC’s unmatched record for innovation that drives societal progress and bolsters the economy.

articles.title_orig: Republican attempts to trip up James Talarico keep backfiring
articles.title_zh: Republican attempts to trip up James Talarico keep backfiring
articles.content_orig:
Democratic state Rep. James Talarico is back in the race for U.S. Senate against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton after spending nine days away from the campaign trail with the flu. NBC 5 Political Reporter Phil Prazan spoke with Talarico in Dallas about his return to campaigning.
State Rep. James Talarico is back on the campaign trail after a nine-day absence due to the flu, dismissing online rumors about his health and challenging Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton to a debate in their U.S. Senate race.
Talarico returned to public events Friday, greeting voters at the Austin City Limits Music Festival, before attending a Kacey Musgraves concert Saturday in Dallas.
Watch NBC 5 free wherever you are
During an interview with NBC 5's Phil Prazan in Dallas, Talarico addressed his recovery, speculation surrounding his absence and his ongoing campaign against Paxton, who defeated incumbent Republican Sen. John Cornyn in the primary.
Create a free account with NBC 5 DFW to save articles and videos.
"Yeah, I got the flu and I'm feeling much better. And I'm glad I had a chance to recover. You know, if you don't take the opportunity to get well, sometimes you can get even sicker," Talarico said. "And so I'm happy we made the decision to just take the week, get better. And now I'm back on the trail."
Talarico, who has previously discussed having diabetes, said he visited his primary care physician but described his illness as nothing worse than a nasty case of the flu.
He said he spent much of his recovery resting in bed and drinking fluids, although his campaign still required him to work from home. He also said he wanted to avoid potentially getting others sick.
Covering politics throughout the state of Texas.
His absence fueled speculation on social media, including claims promoted by some conservatives and Paxton allies that he had experienced a stress-induced episode and was receiving treatment.
Talarico rejected those claims: "That's not true. I just had the flu and I feel much better. But it's a good reminder that you can't believe everything you read on the internet."
With his campaign appearances resuming, Talarico also turned his attention to Paxton and the possibility of a debate between the two Senate candidates.
When asked about President Trump's remarks that Paxton was ready and willing to debate, Talarico said he agreed that the candidates should face off:
"I agree with President Trump. I think Ken Paxton should debate. The president's saying he should debate, FOX News has said he should debate, the people of Texas have said he should debate and I think it's mysterious that Ken Paxton hasn't responded to a request for a debate in 85 days."
Talarico also mocked his opponent, suggesting Paxton's unwillingness to debate was a sign of cowardice.
In a reference to questions about his own health and whereabouts, Talarico ended with a pointed challenge to the attorney general:
"I'm asking for proof of spine from him," said Talarico.
Early voting for the Nov. 3 election runs Monday, Oct. 19 through Friday, Oct. 30.

articles.title_orig: Russia Lab Death Sparks Plague Fears in China
articles.title_zh: Russia Lab Death Sparks Plague Fears in China
articles.content_orig:
Social media speculation that a suspected plague outbreak in Russia could spread to China has reportedly prompted some residents there to stock up on food and supplies.
The U.K.'s Daily Star reported people were scrambling for rice, sugar, eggs, canned food, and other necessities over fears of COVID-style lockdowns.
The report pointed to social media claims rather than any confirmed cases in China.
The Oct. 2 death of a 28-year-old worker at a Russian institute in Irkutsk that studies plagues led to a quarantine response involving at least 200 people.
Russia has denied she died of plague, saying she died of pneumonia.
Dr. Amesh Adalja, a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security in Baltimore, said Sunday on Newsmax the case could involve something more dangerous than plague.
"What worried me was the response of the Russians, the 200 people that were being monitored, the quarantining of a hospital, the hazmat suits," Adalja said on " Wake Up America Weekend ." "That type of reaction made me think this was something worse than plague."
He noted that plague today is "a pretty treatable infection" that does not spread rapidly from person to person.
Adalja also cited the Soviet Union's secret biological weapons program, which he said included its plague research institutes and which "we think has resumed."
The World Health Organization said in a report Saturday that Russia reported negative tests for plague and other high-threat diseases and no additional linked cases, but the cause of death remains undetermined.
Adalja said Russia's denial could be accurate.
"But we still don't know what killed her, what they were testing for, what they were suspicious of," he said. "And I don't know if we'll ever get good answers."

articles.title_orig: Congress Says Webull Is Structurally Tied to China, Stock Craters
articles.title_zh: Congress Says Webull Is Structurally Tied to China, Stock Craters
articles.content_orig:
Hunan Weibu, Webull's mainland China subsidiary, employs 863 people, 62% of its global workforce, according to the House committee, directly contradicting the company's earlier claim of having no PRC-based staff.
A House panel just told millions of Webull users their trading app answers to more than Wall Street. The stock lost nearly a fifth of its value in a single session.
Webull shares opened at $5.15 on October 7. By midday the stock was down as much as 32%. CNBC had reported that the bipartisan House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party had concluded the trading platform is "tied in structural ways" to Beijing. By the close, the stock had pared some of the damage but still finished down roughly 19.1% at $5.89. For a brokerage that leans on retail traders checking balances between work meetings, that's not a bad headline. That's a run on trust.
The committee's report, chaired by Rep. John Moolenaar of Michigan alongside ranking member Raja Krishnamoorthi, didn't accuse Webull of being a shell company. It did something more specific and, for a US-listed app with millions of accounts, more damaging: it laid out a "profound gap" between how Webull presents itself and who actually runs the machine behind it. Moolenaar put it bluntly on CNBC, saying China-based operations "put American investors and their data at risk" because they expose that data to Chinese government authorities.
The specifics are where the report does its real work. According to the committee, Webull's mainland Chinese subsidiary, Hunan Weibu, employs 863 people, which the panel says amounts to 62% of the company's entire global workforce. That number matters because Webull had previously told committee members it "does not have any offices or employees based in the People's Republic of China," a claim the new headcount figure directly contradicts. The committee also flagged software development, data pipelines and core engineering operations. Cross-border data routing, financing and compliance made the list too: all of it dependent on infrastructure governed by Chinese law, meaning Beijing can compel cooperation from the entities that keep the app running.
This isn't a cold case the committee just stumbled into. Moolenaar and Krishnamoorthi first wrote to Webull CEO Anthony Denier back in December 2024. They warned that the company's ties to PRC-based entities raised questions about US user data security and Webull's ability to comply with American regulations. Webull was founded in 2016 under Hunan Fumi Information Technology, a China-based fintech venture started by Wang Anquan, before the company restructured and pushed its public identity toward Florida and New York. The gap between that founding and today's marketing is exactly what the committee spent nearly two years examining.
The Wall Street Journal reported Tesla is weighing a sale or spinoff of its China business to enable a SpaceX merger. Elon Musk called it absurdly fake news. Tesla stock jumped 2.7% overnight and gave most of it back after the denial, leaving investors to decide who to believe. - tesla china spinoff rumors explained - elon musk tesla stock denial impact
Webull disputes the findings. A company spokesperson said Webull "made every effort to cooperate with the Committee, but did not hear from them for more than 20 months before this report was released." The spokesperson called the conclusions "deeply disappointing," citing "significant inaccuracies and unsupported conclusions." The company maintains its US operations run out of its Florida and New York offices, that US customer data sits on US infrastructure, and that access to sensitive systems is controlled domestically.
Here's the problem with that defense: the committee isn't arguing Webull lied about where its American offices sit. It's arguing that the engineering and data plumbing behind the app, the part users never see, runs through a subsidiary Beijing can lean on by law. A US address doesn't settle that question. Neither side disputes that Hunan Weibu exists or that it's large; the dispute is over what that size means for who actually controls the product.
Webull went public through a SPAC merger in April 2025. Since then it's spent the time trying to look like any other US retail brokerage, chasing the same customers as Robinhood and SoFi with zero-commission trades and extended-hours access. A congressional report questioning its structural independence from a foreign adversary government is the kind of headline that outlasts a single trading session. Regulators scrutinizing TikTok set the template here: ownership structure and data routing, not marketing copy, are what Washington is going to keep testing.
For StartupFortune readers weighing retail brokerages or any US-listed fintech with cross-border roots, the Webull episode is a reminder. A Nasdaq listing and a Florida mailing address don't settle questions about who controls the backend. Where the code runs and who can compel the people running it increasingly matters as much as where the logo sits.

articles.title_orig: Massive Anoka pumpkin to be carved into world?s largest jack-o-lantern
articles.title_zh: Massive Anoka pumpkin to be carved into world?s largest jack-o-lantern
articles.content_orig:
Travis Gienger of Anoka, Minnesota, showing off his five championship rings from the World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off. (Safeway World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off / Supplied)
HALF MOON BAY, Calif. (FOX 9) - Minnesota's Travis Gienger won the World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off in California for the fifth time, with his pumpkin, "Rocky", taking home the grand prize.
Rocky weighed in at 2,389 pounds on Monday at the 2026 World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off in Half Moon Bay, California, the heaviest pumpkin in the competition. Rocky also measured 138 inches side-to-side, 131.5 inches end-to-end and 231 inches around.
But Gienger's giant pumpkin didn't break the world record. The current world record for heaviest pumpkin is 2,856 pounds, set on Oct. 3 by a British pumpkin grower. A pumpkin grower in Rhode Island may have surpassed that record on Saturday with his pumpkin that weighed in at 3,156 pounds, although it does not appear that record has been certified yet.
Gienger earned $900 per pound for his pumpkin—which adds up to $2,151.
The city of Anoka is saying go big or gourd home. A champion pumpkin grown in Anoka is expected to break two Guinness World Records this week. Anoka, affectionately known as the Halloween Capital of the World, prides itself on its Halloween celebrations and now has yet another Halloween accolade to celebrate. North America's largest pumpkin is on display at Anoka City Hall, where it will be carved into the world's largest jack-o-lantern by weight and by size on Friday.
This was the 53rd World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off. Gienger has now won the grand prize five times. Here's how his other prize-winning pumpkins compare:
In 2022, Gienger's championship pumpkin, Maverick, was carved into the world's largest jack-o-lantern . The pumpkin was displayed outside Anoka City Hall.
The World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off began in 1974 as a friendly challenge between Half Moon Bay and Circleville, Ohio to see who could grow the biggest pumpkin.
The Source: The 2026 Safeway World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off in Half Moon Bay, California took place on Monday, Oct. 12. The event was livestreamed on YouTube. FOX 9 reported this story from Minnesota.

articles.title_orig: The Single Customer: Who Governs Iran’s Oil Trade with China
articles.title_zh: The Single Customer: Who Governs Iran’s Oil Trade with China
articles.content_orig:
The ChinaMed Project is continuing its research direction dedicated to documenting and analyzing the stakeholders that shape Mediterranean countries’ China policies (for more information on the methodology, see here ). In other words, analyzing the institutional and extra-institutional actors that shape a country’s engagement with China, including how they perceive China and how much influence they wield. Across the Mediterranean, this encompasses a wide range of stakeholders, from foreign ministries and chambers of commerce to armed militias and Chinese diaspora communities.
While data collection is still ongoing, we are happy to present an early snapshot of our findings through a case study authored by Theo Nencini , one of the minds behind this framework. In this article, he analyses how the impact of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran has affected the main actors involved in Iran’s oil trade with China and how they have adapted to the conflict.
When the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran on February 28, 2026, they framed it as a struggle over the country’s political system. In a video address that morning, President Donald Trump told Iranians, “When we are finished, take over your government,” as if regime change were the explicit objective. Within days, Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz . Seven months on, the war has not toppled the regime, but the stakes have changed. The question is no longer whether Iran’s political order will survive, but who will control the conditions under which Persian Gulf oil can reach the global market.
Negotiations over the Strait now dominate the conflict. The fourteen-point Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), signed on June 17, covers a far broader agenda: a cessation of hostilities, sanctions relief for Iranian crude exports and the banking, insurance and transport services attached to them, the release of frozen assets, a $300 billion reconstruction plan and, eventually, the nuclear file. Yet as the military campaign stalled, these issues receded behind the immediate problem of freedom of navigation. Iranian and Omani negotiators, alongside Pakistani mediation, Qatari proposals and indirect U.S. participation, have spent weeks on a transit arrangement, which Tehran makes conditional on further concessions, including compensation for wartime damage.
Only weeks earlier, the trajectory had appeared different. On June 22, five days after the MoU, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), the U.S. Treasury’s sanctions authority, issued General License X , the first broad authorization of transactions in Iranian crude since the 1970s. Covering production, shipping, insurance, and dollar payments, it briefly restored a legal framework for Iranian oil exports. It lasted fifteen days. On July 7, after Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait, OFAC revoked it . American strikes resumed, and the naval blockade of Iranian ports was reimposed on July 14 .
The episode exposed the structure beneath the trade. Iranian crude reaches the market through two systems governed by institutions with different interests and capacities. The formal channel, operated by the Ministry of Petroleum and the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC), holds the statutory monopoly and would gain most from relief, since it depends on legal access to shipping, insurance, banking and counterparties. The parallel channel, operated by the IRGC, thrives precisely where those conditions are lacking. Both deliver into the same market, through intermediaries, transshipment and trading companies that change faster than enforcement can follow.
That market is China, whose regulatory conditions constrain both systems. The Middle East supplied 57% of China’s seaborne crude imports in 2025 , and most crude leaving Hormuz goes to Asia , with China by far the largest single buyer. The closure hit hard: June crude imports fell 41.3% year on year to a decade low, and refinery throughput dropped to its weakest level since 2021. Beijing has called for normal transit to resume, with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi raising the matter with his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi repeatedly .
China nonetheless remained the destination for virtually all Iranian seaborne crude. Kpler data record it as taking 96.2% of Iranian loadings in 2024, 99.8% in 2025, and the entirety from May 2026 onwards. What changed was the volume. The blockade of Iranian ports cut loadings to 271,000 b/d in May 2026, the lowest since June 2020, against a 2025 average of 1.68 million b/d; in July they recovered to about 1.32 million b/d, a fifth below the pre-war level, before the reimposed blockade brought them to zero in September. The war altered how much oil Iran could export, not who bought it.
The continuity conceals a redistribution of control. American sanctions on Iranian oil have been enforced without interruption since 1995-96, European ones from 2012 to 2016 and again since the September 2025 snapback . Their pressure has weakened the Iranian institutions that relied on conventional commercial infrastructure and favored an apparatus able to operate through opaque networks and to shape, by coercion, the environment in which oil moves. The path that led to the war, and the war itself, did not alter Iran’s dependence on China, which sanctions had already entrenched. They may instead have further transformed who, inside Iran, is best positioned to govern it.
This article applies ChinaMed’s China Policy Stakeholder Mapping methodology to analyze this shift. It examines two Iranian stakeholders – the Ministry of Petroleum and NIOC, which retain statutory authority but are losing operational control, and the IRGC, whose sanctions-adapted export system has progressively gained ground on the formal channel – against the Chinese regulatory conditions that determine whether either can keep supplying the Chinese market. The question is not why Iran depends on China, but who , within the Iranian system, increasingly sets the terms on which that dependence yields revenue.
On paper, the Ministry of Petroleum and NIOC remain the sovereign authorities over Iran’s oil sector. In practice, they no longer govern the conditions under which Iranian crude reaches its buyers. The institutions that formally own the oil do not control the networks through which it is sold, transported, and paid for. That gap defines NIOC’s position in the relationship with China.
NIOC’s authority predates the Islamic Republic. The 1974 Petroleum Act entrusted the exercise of national sovereignty over Iran’s petroleum resources exclusively to the company. After the 1979 revolution, a Ministry of Petroleum was created to oversee the sector, and the 1987 Petroleum Act assigned it that sovereignty. But the transfer remained largely formal: for decades, NIOC kept most of its prerogatives.
That ambiguity was resolved in 2011-2012, to the advantage of the IRGC. The Guard’s engineering conglomerate, the Khatam al-Anbiya Construction Headquarters, which grew out of its wartime corps of engineers and was granted a near-monopoly over reconstruction after the Iran-Iraq War (1980-1988), entered the oil and gas sector in the mid-2000s. From 2006, the Ministry awarded it South Pars contracts, some without tender, and sanctions accelerated the trend as foreign partners withdrew: in 2010, phases previously contracted to Shell and Repsol went to an IRGC-led consortium. By May 2012, Khatam al-Anbiya held 51 upstream and downstream contracts. 4
But the decisive shift was institutional. In August 2011, Rostam Ghasemi , Khatam al-Anbiya’s former commander, became Minister of Petroleum. The IRGC gained the stewardship of the body supervising NIOC. In May 2012, the Majles adopted the Law on the Duties and Powers of the Ministry of Petroleum , which subordinated NIOC to the Ministry. articles.title_orig: Nasdaq falls ahead of earnings, economic data while oil rallies
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq falls ahead of earnings, economic data while oil rallies
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures were little changed on Monday night, with traders bracing for a slew of corporate earnings reports from major companies such as JPMorgan Chase and UnitedHealth.
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures rose 30 points. S&P 500 futures hovered around the flatline along with Nasdaq-100 futures .
Big banks JPMorgan , Goldman Sachs , Citigroup and Wells Fargo are slated to release their results before the open on Tuesday. Dow member UnitedHealth is also on deck.
The early reports could set the tone for an earnings season with lofty expectations. Analysts on average expect S&P 500 profits grew by nearly 30% from the year-earlier period, according to FactSet.
"Three groups will likely shape how investors read the season: 1) Banks (consumer and business health), 2) Big Tech (AI monetization), and 3) Energy (the durability of oil-driven profits)," wrote Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise. "Underneath these areas, the health of consumers and businesses amid higher interest rates, elevated costs, and concerns about the macroeconomic environment will be closely monitored across sectors throughout the season."
Investors on Tuesday will also parse through existing home sales figures along with commentary from Federal Reserve officials Christopher Waller, Tom Barkin and Susan Collins.
Later in the week, inflation data for September will be released – which could jolt Treasury yields after they reached multidecade highs recently. The U.S. bond market was closed Monday due to the Indigenous Peoples' Day holiday.
Wall Street is coming off a mixed session. The Dow ended Monday more than 195 points higher, while declines in memory stocks pushed the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 into negative territory for the day.
Big banks JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo are due to report earnings Tuesday before the bell. Here's a peek into what analysts expect:

Shares of Syndax Pharmaceuticals tumbled 15% after the company said axatilimab did not meet its primary endpoint during a Phase 2 trial in which the antibody was used to treat idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
"The MAXPIRe trial did not meet its primary endpoint, and we are disappointed by this outcome given the promising scientific rationale in IPF," said Nick Botwood, head of research & development at Syndax said in a statement.
If the after-hours losses hold through Tuesday's close, it will mark the stock's worst day since May 6, 2025, when it dropped 22%.

articles.title_orig: The sharpest minds of world university sports meet in Liaocheng
articles.title_zh: The sharpest minds of world university sports meet in Liaocheng
articles.content_orig:
Competition is underway as the best student chess and bridge players work to make their way to the podiums.
The Liaocheng 2026 FISU World University Championship Mind Sports opened on the weekend with a captivating opening ceremony. The ceremony featured a wonderful performance that fully incorporated elements of the “Two Rivers” culture, displaying the vitality of the Water City of Liaocheng.
Li Changping, Secretary of the CPC Liaocheng Municipal Party Committee, officially opened the event marking the first time that the FISU Championship Mind Sports is being held in China.
Liaocheng, located in Shandong Province, has earned the nickname “Venice of Northern China” with Dongchang lake a central feature to the city’s beauty.
This host city of 5.9 million residents is building itself as an emerging centre for mind sports. It boasts over 400,000 mind sports enthusiasts along with more than 400 schools that offer chess programs helping mind sports take root in the community.
More than 200 athletes from 21 countries are competing in bridge and chess from 11 to 16 October. The host venue is the Arcadia International Hot Spring Hotel in Liaocheng, with the Dongchang Hall hosting bridge competition and the Fenghuang (Phoenix) Hall welcoming chess.
The hot spring facilities, greenery, and tranquil waterscapes provide a calming and focused environment for all the competing athletes.

articles.title_orig: Starbucks says not buying Chipotle, ends takeover speculation
articles.title_zh: Starbucks says not buying Chipotle, ends takeover speculation
articles.content_orig:
Starbucks on Monday denied it is considering acquiring Chipotle Mexican Grill in what would be the biggest-ever restaurant takeover.
"Starbucks is not buying Chipotle," a Starbucks spokesperson told CNBC's Jim Cramer.
Chipotle's stock was down nearly 4% in morning trading Monday following the statement, while Starbucks shares were 1% higher.
The coffee giant's denial comes after days of rumors about a potential megadeal between the two restaurant companies.
On Thursday, the Financial Times reported that Starbucks had been working with advisors on a Chipotle takeover proposal in recent months. The newspaper cited people familiar with the matter.
Earlier in October, Semafor reported that Chipotle had hired advisors to defend against activist investors or an unwanted takeover bid. The fast-casual chain is trying to recover from a rocky 2025 , when traffic to its restaurants fell. Chipotle shares are down about 20% over the last year, making it a cheaper target.
The deal rumors sent shares of Chipotle higher, while Starbucks stock fell on the reports.
Chipotle investors were looking forward to a potential reunion with Brian Niccol, who previously led Chipotle and is now CEO of Starbucks. But Starbucks shareholders were largely concerned about an expensive distraction while the coffee chain is in the middle of its own turnaround.

articles.title_orig: Teen killed, 24 injured by unexploded Hezbollah munition on hike near Lebanon border
articles.title_zh: Teen killed, 24 injured by unexploded Hezbollah munition on hike near Lebanon border
articles.content_orig:
One teenager was killed and others were wounded, according to Israeli emergency response services, after an explosion on an Israeli school trip near the Lebanon border.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said an initial review by soldiers at the scene indicated that explosion was caused by an unexploded Hezbollah munition that had fallen in the area. It’s unclear when the projectile was fired. Pictures released by the IDF showed a military helicopter evacuating patients for medical treatment.
“Apparently, the suspicion is that an unexploded munition of some kind exploded in the hands of one of the students,” said Deputy Police Commissioner Meir Eliyahu, a commander in Israel’s northern district, according to Reuters.
According to United Hatzalah, an Israeli emergency response service, three people sustained serious injuries in the explosion, while at least 10 others suffered light-to-moderate injuries. The wounded were evacuated to three hospitals in the area, police said.
In a statement, the Ma’alot-Tarshiha municipality in northern Israel said students and staff were on the local school’s annual trip when the explosion happened. The country’s Ministry of Education said it was an “extremely difficult incident, and our thoughts are with the victims and their families.” Commissioner Daniel Levy told Reuters it was a “very serious incident, in which children who went on a field trip were hurt, to our sorrow.”
On Monday evening, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, along with Israel’s education minister, visited the wounded and their families at Rambam Hospital in Haifa. Netanyahu instructed the IDF to reinforce the prohibitions against touching unexploded ordinance.
Shortly after the explosion occurred on Monday afternoon, Israel Police said the initial suspicion was that the explosion was a result of an unexploded munition along the border near the villages of Yiftah and Manara. Bomb disposal experts were dispatched to examine the cause of the explosion, police said.
MDA said it was a “complex incident” as they sent numerous teams to the site. “We quickly dispatched substantial forces to the scene, including ambulances, mobile intensive care units (MICUs), and an MDA helicopter, which was also scrambled to the incident,” said regional director Itzik Shushan.
A US-brokered ceasefire in late-June was supposed to end months of conflict in southern Lebanon as it paved the way for the deployment of the Lebanese military and the gradual withdrawal of the IDF. Israel pulled back from two small areas along the so-called yellow line that demarcates the zone occupied by the Israeli military, but further progress on the agreement has largely stalled.
Israel has razed entire villages in southern Lebanon and has continued to carry out regular strikes there as it tries to remove Hezbollah from the territory.

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: Deadly Houthi attacks keep Saudi airport closed as Trump considers U.S. strikes in Yemen
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Deadly Houthi attacks keep Saudi airport closed as Trump considers U.S. strikes in Yemen
articles.content_orig:
Saudi Arabia has launched an investigation to determine how its air defenses failed to intercept a barrage of missiles and drones fired by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, including an attack on Riyadh airport that killed at least 13 people and wounded over 300, two regional officials said Monday.
The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly, said the initial probe showed that Yemen's Houthis first fired multiple drones to pave the way for a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles to reach Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport.
The Houthis possess ballistic missiles and advanced systems fitted with warheads that can change direction during flight and pose a challenge to Patriot interceptors and other defense systems used by the Saudis.
One of the officials said the investigation also aims to find out why air defense systems did not provide earlier warning of the attack in which the Houthi missiles and drones flew over 620 miles to reach Riyadh.
Delta Air Lines said Monday it is delaying plans for nonstop flights from Atlanta to Riyadh amid escalating attacks between Yemen's Houthi militants and Saudi Arabia.
"The safety and security of our customers and employees always come first and continue to guide our operational decisions," the company said in a statement. "We remain in close contact with relevant government and aviation partners, including Saudia and Riyadh Air, as we monitor the situation."
Delta announced last year its plans to operate nonstop flights to Riyadh three times a week on its Airbus A350-900 aircraft in October 2026. It said at the time that the new destination would help strengthen business and travel ties between the United States and Saudi Arabia.
The company said Monday the launch of Atlanta-Riyadh flights will take place in March 2027.
Iran's Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday denied the U.K.'s allegations that Tehran was involved in last month's security incident at a British base used by American bombers.
In a statement posted to social media , the foreign ministry condemned what it said were "unfounded accusations by the United Kingdom against Iran."
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier Monday the security incident at RAF Fairford — which led to the arrests of seven men who were later released on bail — was "highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran" and "almost certainly" by the regime's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
In its response, Tehran said by using terms like "highly likely" and "almost" certain, the U.K. is "hiding behind vague language without presenting concrete evidence or proof."
Foreign ministers of NATO member countries on Monday issued a joint statement condemning "Iran's use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners."
The statement said the countries recognize the U.K.'s assertion that last month's security incident at RAF Fairford , a U.S.-run air base in Britain, was likely coordinated by Iran.
"Any attempt by Iran to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable," the joint statement said. " Anyone who conducts hostile activities on behalf of Iran, or any other state, should know that we will take action to identify, investigate, disrupt, and prosecute these acts."
In a separate statement, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said he welcomes the statement issued by allies and partners, echoing their denouncement of "Iran's involvement in violence and threats on Allied territory."
"NATO will continue to do its part to safeguard the security of our one billion people across the Alliance," Rutte said.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis claimed an attack targeting Riyadh's international airport on Monday, after a Saudi-led coalition said it had shot down a missile over the capital.
"Our armed forces were able to target (King) Khalid International Airport in the Saudi enemy's capital Riyadh this evening with a ballistic missile and the hit was precise," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said . He said the group also targeted the Khamis Mushait base in the kingdom's south with a drone.
Saree also warned against "the consequences of operating flights toward Saudi airports, as they are not safe, with the exception of the airports and airspace of the sacred areas in Mecca al-Mukarramah and Medina al-Munawwarah."
It's unclear whether there were any injuries.
Several powerful explosions rattled the Saudi capital Riyadh on Monday night, just moments after a text message sent to residents' mobile phones warned of an aerial threat.
"The area is under a hostile aerial threat. Please remain calm, stay indoors or in a safe place away from windows and doors," read the message.
Around the same time, the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said its forces intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Iran-backed group at the capital.
"Interception and destruction of a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh," Major General Turki al-Malki, a spokesperson for the coalition, wrote in a post on X.
U.K. Foreign Minister Ed Miliband announced sanctions against two Iranian nationals on Monday, "for their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas," he said in a statement .
"We will not tolerate threats on British soil," said Miliband, who earlier had released a joint statement alongside his counterparts in the U.S., Australia, Canada and 23 other countries, which condemned hostile activities by Iran on foreign soil.
Their statements followed a security incident at the RAF Fairford air base in southern England, which U.K. government leaders and others have attributed to Iran. Iran denied its involvement Monday in comments released by state media.
The U.S. embassy in Riyadh said on Monday that American citizens had been detained for filming recent events in Saudi Arabia, which has suffered a string of deadly attacks by Yemen's Houthis.
The embassy said "American citizens have been detained for taking photos of recent events," without specifying how many were arrested or whether they had been released. It noted that Saudi authorities have warned that "filming, publishing, or sharing information related to counter missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability."
Several foreign residents in Riyadh have told AFP that acquaintances were detained for filming recent events and sharing the footage on social media.
Iran on Monday denied any involvement in a security incident at England's RAF Fairford air base, which the U.S. previously used to deploy long-range bombers during the war.
"The Iranian ambassador in London, Ali Moussavi, has again categorically rejected the accusations concerning Tehran's role in the incident at the Fairford military base," the Iranian state news agency IRNA reported, adding that he "called on the British government to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any."
That statement followed earlier remarks from British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who said the incident was "almost certainly directed" by Iran's Revolutionary Guard.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Monday to have struck three supertankers in the Strait of Hormuz over the last two days.
The IRGC Navy said in its most recent attack on a ship, Monday, "a third non-compliant super-tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire."
It said the tanker had switched off the system that broadcasts a vessel's location in an effort to evade Iranian restrictions on navigating the strait without permission and "disregarded warnings from the IRGC Navy."

articles.title_orig: PODCAST: Omar raid, diesel deal pushback, prediction markets (Updated)
articles.title_zh: PODCAST: Omar raid, diesel deal pushback, prediction markets (Updated)
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Monday defended last week's decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel fuel exports after the announcement drew bipartisan criticism .
Trump, in a Truth Social post , accused the media of hypocrisy for allegedly refusing to cover past purchases of Russian energy by the European Union.
"The European Union paid Russia 250 Billion Dollars for Energy, and the Fake News Media doesn't want to get near that story," Trump wrote.
While the president did not specify, his figure roughly tracks with some estimates of how much the EU has spent importing fossil fuels from Russia since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The European Commission has launched a plan to phase out its dependence on Russian energy.
"I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!" Trump wrote in the social media post.
Lawmakers from both parties raised concerns about Trump's decision to let Russia supply some diesel to the U.S. and global markets for the next six months.
The plan received pushback from multiple congressional Republicans who have urged Trump not to lift the U.S. ban on energy imports from Russia until its president, Vladimir Putin , ends the war against Ukraine.
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," a group of seven senators, including four Republicans, said in a joint statement on Sunday.
Other Republicans have also raised issues with Trump's deal.
"While I understand the desire to bring down diesel prices, I am concerned the lifting of sanctions on Russian oil will only fund the Kremlin's war machine—emboldening more violence and destruction, as we have seen in recent days," Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas, said Friday.
Trump, whose party is staring down a potentially tough midterm election that has coincided with widespread economic dissatisfaction, says the plan he coordinated with Putin will help bring down sky-high diesel prices. Some analysts say the policy won't make much of a dent , however.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that the U.S. easing sanctions on Moscow "plays into Russia's hands."

This is CNBC's Morning Squawk newsletter. Subscribe here to receive future editions in your inbox.
Happy Monday. I saw "The Social Reckoning" over the weekend, the first of a string of new movies and TV shows focused on technology executives.
Stock futures are little changed this morning. Stocks finished last week higher.
Here are five key things investors need to know to start the trading day:
Following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, President Donald Trump on Friday said that Moscow would supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market. The deal comes as Trump faces pressure to bring Americans relief at the pump before the midterm elections, but analysts are skeptical the agreement will lead to lower prices.
Independent evaluators once occupied a quiet corner of the artificial intelligence world. Now, as safety concerns mount, they're being tapped to help get the industry on the right track.
AI titans are turning to third-party evaluators such as Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR) and Transluce to monitor their models. As CNBC's Ashley Capoot reports, the role of these organizations has become even greater in the absence of a federal government safety framework.
Speaking of AI safety: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella became the latest industry leader to voice concern over AI risks, writing on social media Saturday that the technology needs an "emergency brake." Nadella said models should be built with containment and independent controls.
The Justice Department is investigating whether the White House television press pool violated antitrust laws by suspending their coverage of Trump when the president banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from accessing the White House.
The DOJ said it is looking at whether the press pool's pause in coverage broke the Sherman Act, a federal law prohibiting agreements that unreasonably restrain trade. Members of the press pool — which includes CNN, Fox News, ABC, CBS and NBC — did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.
Meanwhile, Katie Zacharia, a lawyer and conservative commentator, will take over as White House press secretary today. Zacharia succeeds Karoline Leavitt, who left the Trump administration in August and is expected to begin a role at Fox News next month.
CNBC's Morning Squawk recaps the biggest stories investors should know before the stock market opens, every weekday morning.
Subscribe here to get access today .
French bond yields are trading near levels last seen in 2002. Some investors are wondering whether Italy could face a similar fate as the country considers widening its budget deficit.
The Italian government is set to present a budget that includes recently confirmed allocations for defense and energy. The new spending levels could enlarge Italy's deficit over the next two years and make its debt-to-GDP ratio the highest in Europe, according to Goldman Sachs.
As a result, Italy's government bonds could feel more pressure heading into the country's general election next year. Still, some investors see Italy as better off than France thanks to its largely domestic bond ownership.
Retailers are trying to clean up their balance sheets. To do so, many are taking products off of their shelves.
As CNBC's Ryan Baker writes, less inventory can help businesses stabilize sales and reduce the likelihood of ending up with a glut of product. But on the other hand, fewer items leaves shoppers with fewer choices.
That's a compromise many well-known retailers have made amid surging energy and food prices. Brands from Dollar General to BJ's Wholesale Club to Lululemon have all announced plans to reduce the number of products they sell.

articles.title_orig: Shane Gillis’ ‘SNL’ monologue slammed as sexist for comments about women
articles.title_zh: Shane Gillis’ ‘SNL’ monologue slammed as sexist for comments about women
articles.content_orig:
Comedian Shane Gillis drew controversy again for his “Saturday Night Live” monologue Saturday after commenting that he “didn’t know women just dress like whores now” at the gym.
Gillis appeared to draw few laughs from the studio audience after making the remark during the monologue, which marked his third time hosting the NBC sketch comedy show. (“SNL” airs on NBC, a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.)
After lamenting that he needs to lose weight, he went on to describe the “neon, artificial-vape colored” shorts that women are wearing to work out, and the fact that men are not allowed to look at women in those shorts.
The bit drew an outpouring of backlash toward Gillis online, with hundreds of people sharing their negative reactions on TikTok, Instagram, X and Threads.
Representatives for “SNL” and Gillis did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Gillis, who is known for his raunchy style of comedy , has a history of placing women — and other marginalized groups — at the butt of jokes. Many people called it tone-deaf of Gillis to make such comments following the reports around a former Cornell University student who alleged she was gang-raped at an on-campus fraternity house in 2024.
Among the chorus of vocal critics was actor Dan Levy, who on Sunday posted an Instagram video in which he said, “Women wearing short shorts at the gym does not make them whores. It makes the men calling them whores misogynists. There’s a difference there.”
Levy, who created and starred in “Schitt’s Creek,” said he is “speechless that something like that can exist on live national television.”
“And to be perfectly honest,” Levy continued, “more men need to be standing up in opposition to it because it’s complacency that has created the environment with which women are sexually assaulted, and it’s a ‘conversation’ as opposed to a crime.”
Levy called on men to defend women more often and said it is not a women’s issue — “this is an everybody issue,” he added.
“The more that men objectify women in the media, the more that other men see them as objects and treat them as objects,” he said. “They are not objects. They are superior human beings to men.”
Some used Gillis’ monologue to show solidarity for Cornell’s Jane Doe, who accused seven Chi Phi fraternity members of plying her with drugs before sexually assaulting her overnight following a fraternity party.
As the investigation made headlines, women began sharing their own experiences with sexual assault on campus and what they say were inadequate responses from their universities and their police departments, with some coalescing around the hashtag #iamjanedoe.
Writer Jessica Valenti said that she thinks Gillis was probably aware about the “major national conversation happening right now about sexual assault” in relation to the Cornell case.
“This is his contribution to that conversation,” she said. “This is him telling us what he thinks of the discourse on sexual assault. ... That is rape culture.”
Others, like writer and comedian Sophia Benoit , said Gillis’ joke about how women dress at the gym was not funny.
It “has been a very common joke for AT LEAST fifteen years, and it has never once that I can recall been performed with a punchline,” she wrote on X.
Gillis’ career has been fraught with controversy, mainly, his time with “SNL.” He was hired as a cast member in 2019 , before he was quickly canned for previously making racist jokes on his podcast. The criticisms of Gillis piled on when other clips of him using offensive language went viral at the time.
At the time, he apologized but said he would continue to make shocking and taboo jokes.
“We want SNL to have a variety of voices and points of view within the show, and we hired Shane on the strength of his talent as a comedian and his impressive audition for SNL,” a spokesperson for “SNL” executive producer Lorne Michaels told NBC News in 2019. “We were not aware of his prior remarks that have surfaced over the past few days. The language he used is offensive, hurtful and unacceptable.”
The show, which was home to Bowen Yang (the show’s first Asian American cast member ) at the time, chose to fire Gillis, but invited him back to host in 2024 and 2025 before Saturday’s appearance.
Later during Saturday’s episode, Gillis accidentally slipped an f-bomb during a sketch and later apologized. The Federal Communications Commission “prohibits obscene, indecent and profane content from being broadcast on the radio or TV.” The agency defines “profane content” as “grossly offensive” language that is “considered a public nuisance,” according to its website.
Some online pointed out that Gillis apologized for cursing during a sketch but not for offending people during his monologue.
“That’s a pretty ridiculous contrast,” one social media user wrote . “An accidental swear gets an apology, while insulting women is supposed to pass as edgy comedy.”
Rebecca Cohen is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Victims of Pennsylvania mass shooting included pregnant daughter of gunman
articles.title_zh: Victims of Pennsylvania mass shooting included pregnant daughter of gunman
articles.content_orig:
The victims of a mass shooting in northwest Pennsylvania included the gunman’s wife and pregnant daughter, who was due to give birth Monday, authorities said.
Matthew Stone , 45, died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound Friday after he opened fire at his home on Perry Street in Erie, Erie County Coroner Lyell Cook told NBC News on Monday.
Victims included Stone’s wife, Michelle Stone, 44; daughter, Angelina K. Stone, 24, who was pregnant; and sons Matthew Stone Jr., 21, and Jonathan Stone, 19, Cook said.
Angelina Stone was carrying “an unborn fetus who was supposed to have been born today,” Cook said.
Two other unidentified children, a 5-year-old boy and a nearly 2-year-old girl, who were also related to the shooter were killed inside the house, according to the coroner.
All six of those victims were found in the house, where they lived, while victims Twila A. Tanner, 51, and Lora Lee Roberts, 37, were fatally shot outside, Cook said.
Roberts was Michelle Stone’s sister and had gone to the house Friday at the request of Angelina Stone, who needed a ride to the hospital, said the victim’s friend Christine Tombaugh.
Tanner was a friend and neighbor of Roberts, and they lived just a few miles from the crime scene, Tombaugh said.
Roberts was active in local homeless advocacy work, so answering a relative’s call for help and bringing along a friend for assistance was typical of her kindness, Tombaugh said.
“Absolutely, that’s who she was,” said Tombaugh, executive director of the homeless shelter Community of Caring .
“Her passion in life was helping others. She had a giving spirit, a beautiful heart,” Tombaugh said. “Great mom, just a valued friend. She had a heart for the homeless and people in need, just helping whoever she could. That was her passion.”
Juicesiyah Alexander Ezekiel , the slain girl’s father, said he is struggling to understand why the elder Stone opened fire.
“I wouldn’t even put this on my worst enemy, man,” Ezekiel told NBC affiliate WICU of Erie. “It’s sickening.”
The girl was going to turn 2 next month.
“Her name is Amari’anna,” Ezekiel said. “She’s the most beautiful baby God could have created.”

articles.title_orig: Louis Vuitton Trademark Dispute Leads to Sales Slump in China
articles.title_zh: Louis Vuitton Trademark Dispute Leads to Sales Slump in China
articles.content_orig:
Luxury retail company LVMH saw quarterly sales slump following a trademark dispute in China.
Organic revenue for the company’s fashion and leather goods unit fell 5% year over year in the third quarter, LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton announced in a Monday (Oct. 12) press release, with the company’s total revenue for the quarter up 1%.
Louis Vuitton sales suffered in China after the company achieved a victory in a trademark battle with local tea company Molly Tea , Bloomberg reported Monday. This led to backlash from Chinese consumers, angry that the world’s biggest luxury company would take a much smaller merchant to court.

Sales in the region including China dipped 5% in the quarter, the report said, marking the only area where LVMH saw negative performance, the report said. The company’s American depositary receipts dropped as much as 3.6% in New York following the release of the numbers.
LVMH’s stock is down more than 40% this year, on pace for the company’s worst yearly performance since 2008’s global financial crisis, according to the report. Although much of the industry is seeing a downturn in demand, LVMH’s stock is the worst performer this year among major luxury names, followed by rival Hermes .
Gucci’s revenue fell 5% on a comparable basis in the first half of 2026, including a 6% drop at directly operated stores, PYMNTS reported Sept. 17. Second-quarter comparable revenue was still down 2% despite an uptick from the first quarter. Kering Fashion & Leather Goods, which includes Gucci and several other houses, fell 1% comparably for the half.
Department stores were working to get customers “to spend more without making the jump into luxury,” according to the report, which cited increased sales at Macy’s and Dillard’s .
“For department stores, the difference between moving upmarket and moving into luxury is consequential to the size of the customer base they can address,” the report said.
Meanwhile, the PYMNTS Intelligence report “ The Smart Basket Opportunity: Why Issuers Are Ready For A Better Rewards System ” found in June that 56% of issuers and FinTechs said their card rewards increased average spend per transaction, 61% said they boosted total spending and 66% reported an increase in card use frequency.

articles.title_orig: Energy prices rise after Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ fails to move Russia or Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Energy prices rise after Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ fails to move Russia or Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Oil and gas prices rose Monday after an “energy ceasefire” announced by President Donald Trump on Sunday failed to gain traction.
Brent crude oil jumped 2% to almost $108 per barrel and U.S. crude oil rose more than 2% to about $94. Meanwhile, diesel futures fully erased a small drop they saw last week.
Just weeks out from the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the price pressures are mounting. Republicans face a steep climb to maintain their majorities in Congress, and voters across the country cite high gas prices as a key issue affecting their votes.
The average nationwide price of diesel fuel Monday was $6.26 per gallon, nearly 80% higher than it had been at the start of the year, according to AAA data.
The rising prices Monday came less than 24 hours after Trump declared that a ceasefire had been agreed to.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump wrote on Truth Social .
Shortly after the president’s post, Russia renewed strikes against Ukrainian energy assets.
Pressed by reporters Monday as to why neither the Kremlin nor Kyiv had firmly committed to his ceasefire, Trump indicated that he knew when he made the announcement on Sunday that he did not yet have a commitment from either side.
“They agreed, you know why? Because I said ‘You agree,” Trump told reporters at the White House. As for getting Russian President Vladimir Putin to commit, Trump said, “We’re going to see what happens.”
Asked if he was aware that Russia had already violated the ceasefire Trump had announced, the president replied, “I’m not sure about that,” before claiming there had been “violations on both sides.”
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine learned about Trump’s ceasefire from media reports and was given no advance warning. He reiterated his position that Ukraine was open to an agreement not to target enemy energy infrastructure as long as Moscow agrees to it, too.
In the meantime, Russia continued with “glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said Monday, noting that a power plant in Kharkiv had recently been attacked.
“Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps. Putin had one answer to all of them — ‘nyet,’” Zelenskyy said, using the Russian word for “no.”
The Kremlin on Monday neither confirmed nor denied having agreed to a deal.
Trump’s Sunday announcement closely mirrored a similar post he made in September, when he announced that “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!”
There, too, Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s participation hinged on Russia’s agreement to comply, which never came. Neither Ukrainian nor Russian strikes on the other’s energy assets slowed down in September.
The dubious ceasefire Trump declared over the weekend followed a stunning announcement Friday in which the president said Russia would supply millions of barrels of diesel “to the American and Global Marketplace.”
The announcement came after a phone call Friday between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin that reportedly lasted over an hour.
Trump said the deal with Putin would “immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace.” That would translate into about 2.25 million barrels of diesel, or less diesel than the United States uses in just one day.
Further details and logistics of Russia’s plan had yet to be announced Monday.
In addition to the Russia deal, Trump has pressured G7 allies to release more diesel fuel supplies in recent days and lifted domestic restrictions on an off-road variety of diesel.
In order to clear a legal path for the diesel deal, the Treasury Department announced a six-month suspension of the fuel sanctions imposed on the Kremlin in 2022 for its illegal invasion of Ukraine.
Ukrainian officials, European allies and some U.S. lawmakers were aghast at the deal and the U.S. decision to unilaterally ease Russia sanctions.
Trump defended the deal Monday , calling it “the right choice for the American People.”
Trump also said more diesel fuel would be made available “within a short period of time,” if Russia’s refineries could produce it.
Yet experts are highly skeptical that there will be any significant resumption of Russian diesel exports in the near term.
Due to Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia , refiners that produce oil, gas and diesel have suffered heavy damage.
“Reported gasoline output is down by 20% compared with 2025 levels, while diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30%, prompting the government to restrict fuel exports to protect domestic supplies,” analysts at the International Energy Agency wrote in a September report.
For weeks, Trump has focused on the price of diesel fuel, which began rising as a result of the Iran war that the U.S. and Israel launched in February.
In July, escalations in the Russia-Ukraine war began adding to the pressure on diesel prices.
As Ukrainian drones systematically targeted Russian energy assets, the Kremlin responded by restricting diesel exports in order to preserve its supply for domestic use.
Until then, Russia had been one of the world’s top exporters of refined oil products, which include diesel fuel.
Russia said Friday that it would lift some of its export restrictions in order to accommodate the deal with Trump. But it was unclear how fast that would happen.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Trump's top NATO general: 'We will fight' if Russia attacks Europe
articles.title_zh: Trump's top NATO general: 'We will fight' if Russia attacks Europe
articles.content_orig:
He said it’s 'up to our people' in response to Trump’s call for new elections.
After President Donald Trump demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy defended the attacks in an exclusive interview with ABC News, saying his country is responding to repeated Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
"I said it to President Trump … to his team and to his people several times: we want peace, we are ready for [a] ceasefire, we are ready to begin from any kind of steps of de-escalation," Zelenskyy told "This Week" co-anchor Jonathan Karl. "And if the Russians want us not [to] attack their diesel, their refineries and etc., we are asking President Trump, give them signal not attack energy infrastructure of Ukraine."
He went on, "Don't attack us. Don't kill our children. We will stop attack[ing] your diesel. And I think it's [a] fair, fair deal."
After Zelenskyy’s interview on ABC News aired, Trump said on social media that Ukraine and Russia had both agreed to an energy ceasefire.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” his post said.
Zelenskyy and his office were not informed about Trump’s statement of an energy ceasefire with Russia ahead of time and learned about it from social media, a senior source in Ukraine's presidential office told ABC News.
The source said Ukraine has no information about the alleged agreement.
On Saturday, Trump lashed out at Zelenskyy to reporters, claiming the Ukrainian president "chooses not to" end the war with Russia, which began when Russia invaded the sovereign country in February of 2022.
Amid a global energy crisis, Trump took issue with Ukraine's repeated strikes on Russian oil refineries, asserting that those strikes are exacerbating the price of diesel.
"We said you could do whatever you want to Russia, don't hit the refineries, because that's a world problem that's caused. And [Zelenskyy] wants to make problems for the world," Trump said. "He can do whatever he wants. But you can't do that because we have a world problem. And the problem is caused by the lack of refineries for diesel fuel. So what does he do? He goes and hits refineries."
A senior Ukrainian source told ABC News that Ukraine expects the Trump administration to stop sharing U.S. intelligence that tracks Russian missile launches in retaliation over Kyiv’s refusal to end strikes on Russia’s oil industry.
Trump and Zelenskyy have had a tumultuous relationship. In 2025, a meeting in the Oval Office with reporters devolved into a shouting match before the cameras, with Trump and Vice President JD Vance rebuking the Ukrainian president for his handling of the war and even falsely blaming Zelenskyy for beginning the conflict.
The latest spat comes after Trump announced the U.S. had made a deal with Russia to "immediately" import 300,000 tons of its diesel fuel, with a promise that millions more are coming.
Zelenskyy said this deal amounts to an "obvious weakness."
"It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said. "We count on America’s fair support for our defense of life, for our defense of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one."
Less than 24 hours later, Trump called for Zelenskyy to be replaced.
"You know what I suggest? I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal. Because he could have made many deals. And for some reason, he never does," Trump said on the White House South Lawn. "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."
He later told reporters, "I think he should have an election."
Responding to those comments, Zelenskyy told Karl, "With all respect to President Trump, it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader."
Zelenskyy also offered a solution that he said was shared with the Trump administration: a commitment to hold elections if Russian President Vladimir Putin abides by a 60-day ceasefire.
“I know that Putin wanted very much to change the president in Ukraine, I understand it. And if President Trump really wants to have some changes in -- during elections, I also shared it with his team: please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections. Of course, we will be ready for any choice of our people.”
Karl asked Zelenskyy why he thinks Trump and Elon Musk, whose Starlink internet is essential for Ukraine, are blaming him for the war’s continuation. Musk said Saturday on X that Zelenskyy has “gone too far.”
“Because these people can't find a key how to stop Putin,” Zelenskyy said. “Because it's more simple to speak about the prices and connect it with Ukraine when everybody in the world understands ... prices are rising … because of the war in Middle East, of the blocking of Hormuz, because of these reasons. Everybody understands it.”
Asked how long Ukraine can continue to defend itself as the war approaches five years, Zelenskyy said the war has to end.
“I hope that we will save this unity, Europe and the United States," he said. "We will defend ourselves because otherwise, we will lose our life and homes, our freedom, independence, Ukraine. Yeah, we can't lose it. And the truth is on our side."
