articles.title_orig: The US needs its own grey-zone tactics in the South China Sea - The Strategist | ASPI's analysis and commentary site
articles.title_zh: The US needs its own grey-zone tactics in the South China Sea - The Strategist | ASPI's analysis and commentary site
articles.source: The Strategist | ASPI's analysis and commentary site
articles.content_orig:
Passive resistance to Beijing’s actions in the South China Sea is not working. If the United States wants to win in the region, it needs a grey-zone strategy of its own.
Beijing has spent a decade refining a playbook that stays deliberately below the threshold of armed conflict. Chinese coast guard ships ram Philippine vessels, maritime militia swarm disputed reefs, and drones shadow foreign ships. Washington’s response – patrols, joint statements and expressions of concern – has imposed few costs and changed little.
This passivity means that China isn’t being deterred. Indeed, it’s being reassured that it can keep getting away with what it’s doing.
The US doesn’t need ships built for ramming to change that calculation. Rather, it should play to its strengths: a vast intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance network, powerful cyber and electromagnetic warfare capabilities and a web of regional partners. The US military’s F3EAD targeting cycle (find, fix, finish, exploit, analyse and disseminate) offers a template for response. For grey-zone competition, it can be adapted into F2RED: find, fix, respond, exploit and disseminate, with calibrated non-kinetic responses replacing the kinetic component (the ‘finish’).
The first two steps of the cycle that could be applied to the South China Sea are largely in place. Intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance assets across the region already track Chinese coast guard, navy, and maritime militia vessels, and coordination with partner forces can expand the network even further. But after that there’s a gap, because of Washington’s reticence to respond with any operation that may cause escalation.
One response below the threshold of armed conflict is to apply soft-kill effects – that is, nothing with kinetic impact, at least not on anything very costly or with people in it. When Chinese vessels launch uncrewed aircraft to harass or surveil ships of US partners, allied forces can jam or bring down the drones on the spot. Operations can be conducted against Chinese drones elsewhere to divert Beijing’s attention from the area of tension. The same tools become more potent against larger, more expensive ships and aircraft. Crucially, these effects must be paired with signalling, making it clear to Beijing that if its vessels don’t break contact with partners, costs will follow.
Cyber is a second channel for imposing costs. Beyond highlighting Chinese cyber actions against the US and its partners, the US can integrate offensive cyber capabilities into the ‘respond’ phase. By imposing proportionate costs on Chinese government, military or coast guard entities or networks, the US can signal that continued Chinese grey-zone actions will have consequences. For example, if a Chinese vessel rams a Philippine ship, the US could respond by disrupting critical systems associated with Chinese maritime operations. Because such capabilities can be employed from outside the immediate area of a dispute, they also provide strategic depth and another means of responding to Chinese coercion.
The US Coast Guard and Navy can work alongside partner coast guards to block, stop, and arrest militia or fishing crews caught operating illegally in partner waters. The principle is simple: partners enforce their own laws in their own waters, with US ships and intelligence backing them. This must stay strictly legal and be confined to those breaking international law and the law of US partners. Done properly, it turns Beijing’s favoured tactic, coercion dressed as law enforcement, back on itself, but from firmer legal ground.
Financial tools should be tied to response options. In 2022, the US Treasury sanctioned Chinese distant-water fishing companies , adding more than 150 vessels to the Specially Designated Nationals list over human rights abuses and illegal fishing. Extending that precedent to illegal fishing and militia activity within the region would mean freezing assets and persuading banks to cut their ties, further complicating militia and fishing operations and imposing additional costs.
The last two steps in the chain – exploiting and disseminating – are where the US holds its greatest advantage. It already operates extensively with regional partners, so the infrastructure for sharing information exists. It simply needs to be expanded to countries bullied by China.
That should include tracking data. If China can ram Philippine ships in Philippine waters, Manila should receive the information it needs to enforce its own rights, lawfully, in waters that Beijing claims. That should involve all of the aforementioned strategies supported by US capabilities – enforcing exclusive economic zones by arresting illegal fishing vessels, partnering with the US to jam Chinese drones within those areas, or using US intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance networks to identify and remove Chinese intelligence and surveillance sensors within partners’ territories.
A US–China hotline could accompany all of this, alerting Beijing before the response phase commences and giving it a chance to back down.
Critics will warn that all this would risk escalation, and in the short term some friction would be likely. But Beijing currently pays nothing for testing its neighbours, and it will keep testing them until it pays much more. Demonstrating resolve, rather than tacitly accepting Chinese sovereignty claims, is more likely to lead to de-escalation over time.
Additionally, many regional states dislike China’s bullying but lack the resources to resist it alone. Seeing Washington finally impose costs, lawfully and alongside partners, could stiffen the resolve of those fence-sitters. In grey-zone competition, passivity is a strategy that’s working in Beijing’s favour.
William ‘Billy’ Price is a Major in the United States Marine Corps Reserve, has deployed to the Middle East and Africa as an intelligence officer, and has a master’s in International Service from American University.

articles.title_orig: “That's just insane.” Elephant dies in South Africa – and scientists are stunned at what happens next
articles.title_zh: “That's just insane.” Elephant dies in South Africa – and scientists are stunned at what happens next
articles.content_orig:
Elephants continue to influence the savannah long after they die, new study finds.
In 2009, a large, lone elephant called Alexander died beside a road in South Africa’s Kruger National Park. Over the next few months, researcher Dave Thompson watched what happened to the carcass and wondered how it was affecting the savannah.
Now, research inspired by that thought has found that elephant carcasses can continue to shape ecosystems for years.
Thompson passed Alexander’s body regularly, en route to a different project. “Watching the decomposition of that carcass got me curious,” says Thompson, from the South African Environmental Observation Network. So, a project was born.
In life, elephants are ecosystem engineers . When they munch plants, fell trees, disperse seeds, fertilise the soil and trample the ground, they create opportunities for other species to thrive. But what happens to that influence when an elephant dies?
When a whale dies and sinks to the bottom of the ocean, its carcass can become a rich source of nutrients, sustaining life for decades. Thompson wondered if something similar was happening on land.
To find out, researchers studied elephant carcasses of different ages, measuring changes in the soil, microbes, plants and grazing animals around them. The results are published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences .
Initially, plant life was snuffed out. Nutrients from the body leached into the ground, affecting the soil chemistry. Around fresh carcasses, nitrogen concentrations were up to 3,000 times higher than normal. “That amount of ammonium was not on my bingo card,” says Tercia Midzi, who works at Kruger National Park. Levels were so high that plants struggled to grow.
Soil-dwelling bacteria were affected too. Although their diversity went down, the activity of those that survived rocketed, as a few fast-growing species became dominant.
Plants showed a similar pattern. Once the soil chemistry mellowed, plant diversity remained low, with a handful of nutritious, fast-growing species taking over. The carcass “turns these grasses from watery iceberg lettuce into a juicy romaine,” says Deron Burkepile from UC Santa Barbara.
This did not go unnoticed. Herbivores repeatedly returned to feed on the nutritious grasses, while their manure added yet more nutrients to the soil.
The effects persisted for at least eight years, revealing a previously overlooked way that elephants shape ecosystems.
“It was such a powerful reminder that what we see in nature is often shaped by legacies from the past,” says Izak Smit from South African National Parks, “even when the causes of those legacies have long since disappeared from view.”

articles.title_orig: Archbishop of the US military says Catholic soldiers should not serve on firing squad
articles.title_zh: Archbishop of the US military says Catholic soldiers should not serve on firing squad
articles.content_orig:
The archbishop for the U.S. military says any Catholic service members who are assigned to participate in the livestreamed firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan should ask to be excused — the latest pushback against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's plan.
Archbishop Timothy P. Broglio released a statement Monday to "express my disapproval of what is proposed regarding the execution of the terrorist Hasan," referring to Hegseth's announcement last week that Hasan's execution in December would be publicly viewable.
Broglio pointed to the Catholic Church's opposition to the death penalty. He also warned of "moral injury" to service members who are tasked with carrying out the execution, and asked: "Do we really want to imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries?"
"The US military generally enjoys a good reputation in the world," wrote Broglio. "Is there really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheel chair to the whole world? Does this decision reflect the dignity of the human person?"
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Three days earlier, Pope Leo XIV wrote on social media that the death penalty is "inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person." The pope did not explicitly reference Hasan's planned execution or the botched lethal-injection execution of Christa Pike in his post, which coincided with the World Day Against the Death Penalty.
Hegseth said last week the military plans to make the execution public "because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."
In 2013, Hasan was convicted by court-martial and sentenced to death for killing 13 people and injuring more than 30 at the Army installation in Fort Hood, Texas. The former Army psychiatrist acknowledged at trial that he was responsible for the shooting, claiming he opened fire on fellow service members in an attempt to protect Islamic insurgents from the U.S. military.
Hasan's case could mark the U.S. military's first execution of an American since 1961, and its first use of a firing squad since 1945. Firing squads are also rare in civilian courts.
Publicly viewable executions are virtually unheard of in modern U.S. history: The country's last large-scale public execution appeared to take place 90 years ago, when Rainey Bethea was hanged for rape in front of a crowd of about 20,000 in Kentucky. Other countries that are believed to carry out public executions include Iran, Afghanistan and North Korea .
Hegseth's plan to livestream the execution has drawn criticism from members of both parties, including a growing number of congressional Republicans . Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska said "I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America," and Sen. Kevin Cramer of North Dakota said the "death penalty is not entertainment."
House Speaker Mike Johnson told CBS News some of his House Republican colleagues have "concerns," which he plans to bring to the White House.
"The concern would be that you would create a video that would be a recruiting tool for future terrorists. You know, we've got to think through the policy implications of all that," Johnson told CBS News' Robert Costa . "I wouldn't be watching it if it was aired. But there's a lot of opinions on that. I think there's still some time to talk about that."
Vice President JD Vance, who is Catholic, told reporters last week that "if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."
Eleanor  Watson contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Agents search Rep. Omar's Washington home in criminal probe as she vows she won't 'be silenced'
articles.title_zh: Agents search Rep. Omar's Washington home in criminal probe as she vows she won't 'be silenced'
articles.content_orig:
Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., early Monday morning, a source familiar with the operation told Fox News Digital.
EXCLUSIVE: The home of Rep. Ilhan Omar , D-Minn, was raided early Monday morning by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), a source familiar with the matter told Fox News Digital.
Multiple federal agents with HSI jackets were seen outside Omar's Washington, D.C. home in the early hours of Monday.
Two sources close to the investigation say the search stems from a criminal fraud investigation into the Somali-born congresswoman's immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child.
Omar responded to the raid on X, slamming it as a way for President Donald Trump to "target political enemies" with "baseless lies," and insisted: "I will not be silenced."
Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., early Monday morning, a source familiar with the operation told Fox News Digital. (Andrew Murray/Fox News Digital)
OMAR'S GOP CHALLENGER COMES OUT FIRING WITH VOW TO CLEAN UP 'MESS' IN DEEP BLUE DISTRICT: 'PEOPLE ARE FED UP'
The raid of the Somali-born congresswoman's home started around 6 a.m. with HSI and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) leading the operation. The Department of Justice (DOJ) is also involved in the investigation.
"Today in the Washington, D.C., area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation," a DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital.
The DOJ later added that the investigation was "criminal" in nature.
HSI is the principal investigative arm of DHS. Its scope includes investigating cross-border crime and global threats, including human trafficking and child sexual exploitation, drug smuggling and cybercrime. HSI plays a major front-line role in America’s counterterrorism operations.
A spokesperson for Omar did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. The White House and DHS spokespeople declined to provide comment.
Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on October 12, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Andrew Leyden/Getty Images)
Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) raided the Washington, D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on Monday morning, a source familiar with the operation told Fox News Digital. (Fox News Digital/Andrew Murray)
"I’m ok," Omar wrote on X hours after the search commenced. "Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement."
"For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," she continued. "This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced."
In a post from her official government X account from just after 1:30 p.m., Omar elaborated further.
"This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies. For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," she said.
"Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."
The Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) Minnesota says it will hold a rally in support of Omar Monday afternoon.
"Later today, CAIR-Minnesota and community partners will join a rally in solidarity with Congresswoman Omar, reaffirming the community’s commitment to standing against racism, political intimidation, and attacks on democratic representation," CAIR-Minnesota Executive Director Jaylani Hussein said in a statement.
Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on October 12, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Andrew Leyden/Getty Images)
President Donald Trump's Border Czar Tom Homan said in mid-September that the progressive congresswoman was subject to an ongoing "criminal" investigation, but did not specify the nature of the probe.
WATCH: OMAR SILENT WHEN CONFRONTED ON ALLEGED TIES TO MASSIVE MINNESOTA FRAUD SCANDAL
Omar has been under fire for months and faced a myriad of controversies during her time in Congress. Most recently, her financial disclosures have come into focus.
In 2024, the congresswoman reported that her husband possessed between $6 million and $30 million in assets.
A more recent 2025 financial disclosure report shows Omar’s revised value of shared assets between her and husband to sit at a maximum of $125,000 — a multimillion-dollar drop from the year prior, a difference of about 29.9 million. The lower estimate of their assets, $20,000, compared to the low and high debt estimates, $30,000 and $100,000, would imply the Minnesota Democrat could have a negative net worth.
Rep. Ilhan Omar calls out President Trump and Elon Musk for handling of USAID while also accusing the president of running a dictatorship. (Pool)
ILHAN OMAR'S OFFICE SAYS SHE'S ‘NOT A MILLIONAIRE’ AFTER $30M FILING REVISED DOWN TO UNDER $100K: REPORT
Both she and her husband have separate debts, each ranging somewhere between $15,000 and $50,000 — from her own student loans and her husband’s credit card debt, according to the disclosures.
Omar has repeatedly refused to clarify the disclosures.
During her tenure in Congress, she has been plagued by allegations that she married her brother in 2009 in an alleged immigration fraud scheme.
A federal prosecutor recently told Fox News Digital that the statute of limitations could hinder an investigation into that matter.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Additionally, Omar made headlines this summer after her son's residence was raided in connection to allegations his felon roommate possessed illegal firearms and ammunition.
Fox News' Hannah Brennan contributed to this report.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Dr Fradley on Real-World Atrial Fibrillation and Cardiovascular Outcomes in CLL
articles.title_zh: Dr Fradley on Real-World Atrial Fibrillation and Cardiovascular Outcomes in CLL
articles.content_orig:
Michael G. Fradley, MD, discusses real-world data on atrial fibrillation incidence and its cardiovascular and health care impact in CLL.
Michael G. Fradley, MD, a professor of clinical medicine (cardiovascular medicine), section chief of Consultative Cardiology, and medical director of the Thalheimer Center for Cardio-Oncology at Penn Medicine, discussed real-world data presented on the incidence of atrial fibrillation (AFib) in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) or small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), and its effect on cardiovascular outcomes and health care resource utilization.
In a retrospective study , data from which were presented at the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting , Fradley and colleagues used the US Symphony Health open claims database, which captures both privately insured and Medicare populations, Fradley explained. Among 233,362 patients with newly diagnosed CLL/SLL, 13.1% developed AFib within 1 year of diagnosis. Baseline characteristics did not differ significantly between patients who did and did not develop AFib, he noted.
However, patients who developed AFib (n = 30,518) had higher rates of stroke (14.3% vs 8.9%), bleeding events (27.9% vs 19.1%), and heart failure (54.5% vs 18.9%) than those who did not (n = 202,844; all, P < .0001).
In an exploratory analysis of 22,636 patients who started frontline treatment with a BTK inhibitor, Fradley noted that prior data suggest that AFib rates are highest with the first-generation agent ibrutinib (Imbruvica) and lower with acalabrutinib (Calquence) and zanubrutinib (Brukinsa). In this cohort, AFib occurred in 16.0% of patients treated with ibrutinib (n = 15,325), 13.0% of those treated with acalabrutinib (n = 5447), and 11.0% of those treated with zanubrutinib (n = 1864; P < .0001). The analysis is not definitive but is hypothesis generating, he added.
The lower AFib rate with zanubrutinib also translated to fewer cardiovascular adverse effects among patients who developed AFib, according to Fradley. Among patients with AFib, 4.8% of those treated with zanubrutinib had a stroke vs 12.2% of those treated with ibrutinib.
Fradley also highlighted the resource utilization findings, noting that AFib places a significant financial burden on the health care system. Patients with CLL who developed AFib had significantly greater outpatient, inpatient, and other medical service use than those who did not ( P < .0001).

articles.title_orig: Lindstrom, Polish, Sternfeld and Tabansky pushing for honors at World Para Series Stage 4
articles.title_zh: Lindstrom, Polish, Sternfeld and Tabansky pushing for honors at World Para Series Stage 4
articles.content_orig:
SANTIAGO, Chile – Four archers from the United States are this week in South America for Stage 4 of the inaugural Hyundai World Archery Para Series, which runs from Wednesday until Sunday.
Leading the U.S. team is 2024 Paralympic champion, Jason Tabansky (pictured above). He is joined in the W1 division by Ryan Lindstrom. Karen Sternfeld will look to continue her upward trajectory in para recurve women following appearances in Thailand, Czech Republic and India. The quartet is completed by three-time Paralympian, KJ Polish in para compound men.
Sternfeld has featured at all three previous stages, while Tabansky has competed at two and both Lindstrom and Polish at one. Tabansky took silver in Thailand back in April, before securing gold in Stage 2, held in Nove Mesto, Czech Republic.
Polish was top seed in compound men in Nove Mesto, before losing his quarterfinal contest to eventual bronze medalist, Nathan MacQueen (GBR), via a shootoff.
Sternfeld’s qualification scores have steadily improved throughout the year. She posted 462 in Thailand, before scoring 553 in Czech Republic and then 564 in India.
Lindstrom (pictured), meanwhile, registered a personal best score of 616 in qualification in Czech Republic. The 42-year-old from Florida is still relatively new to international archery. He only made the decision to compete after watching Tabansky win gold in Paris two years ago, and though a podium regular on the national circuit, Lindstrom is fully aware of what it will take to challenge internationally.
“The biggest difference to me is obviously the pressure turns up a bit but that's OK because it helps me focus,” he explained. “My two best scores were shot at international tournaments.
“Competing at this level I feel it truly solidifies the feeling that I'm competing with the best in the world rather than just showing up and shooting at a tournament. That's a really cool feeling.”
Lindstrom won bronze at the 142nd USA Target Nationals and silver at the 2026 U.S. Open, which took place in Springfield, Mo. in August. Since then, the focus has been finishing the year strong.
He added, “I have been using the rest of the outdoor season in the states as practice and training. I’ve been trying different techniques and equipment, including traveling to San Antonio to do some fine tuning, which I feel went really well.”
This is the fourth of five stages in the inaugural World Para Series. The fifth and final stage is in Dubai, UAE from December 5-10.
You can follow the scores, results and progress of the four U.S. archers, with medal matches taking place across Saturday and Sunday.
From Chile, all four USA archers head to Lima, Peru for the 2026 Para Pan American Championships, and a much larger U.S. consisting of 17 athletes. This event runs from October 21-27, with quota spots available for the 2027 Para Pan Am Games, which are also in Lima, Peru next August.

articles.title_orig: Resmetirom Tied to Lower MACE vs Semaglutide in Real-World MASLD Analysis
articles.title_zh: Resmetirom Tied to Lower MACE vs Semaglutide in Real-World MASLD Analysis
articles.content_orig:
A propensity-matched TriNetX analysis presented at ACG 2026 found lower MACE and mortality with resmetirom vs semaglutide over 2 years in MASLD/MASH.
Patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) or metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and hepatic fibrosis who received resmetirom had lower rates of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and all-cause mortality than matched patients receiving semaglutide, according to findings from a real-world analysis presented at the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) 2026 Annual Scientific Meeting in Nashville, Tennessee. 1
The poster, presented by Jalal Samhoun, MD, Florida Atlantic University, addresses a gap the investigators identified: there are no comparative cardiovascular outcome data between the 2 therapies, even though cardiovascular disease contributes heavily to morbidity and mortality in MASLD and MASH. 1
Resmetirom is an oral, liver-directed, thyroid hormone receptor-β agonist. In March 2024, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted it accelerated approval for noncirrhotic MASH with moderate to advanced fibrosis. It was the first drug approved for the disease. In the phase 3 MAESTRO-NASH trial, MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis occurred in 25.9% and 29.9% of patients receiving resmetirom 80 mg and 100 mg, respectively, versus 9.7% with placebo. Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol fell by 13.6% and 16.3% at week 24. 2
Semaglutide 2.4 mg received accelerated approval for the same population in August 2025 based on part 1 of the phase 3 ESSENCE trial, in which 62.9% of patients receiving semaglutide achieved steatohepatitis resolution without worsening of fibrosis, versus 34.3% with placebo. 3 Unlike resmetirom, semaglutide has a dedicated cardiovascular outcome trial. In SELECT, it reduced MACE by 20% versus placebo in adults with established cardiovascular disease and overweight or obesity without diabetes. 4
Investigators used the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network to identify adults with MASLD or MASH and hepatic fibrosis receiving resmetirom or semaglutide. They performed 1:1 propensity score matching on demographics, cardiovascular risk factors, metabolic comorbidities, liver disease characteristics, medications, and laboratory values. 1
The final cohorts included 4253 patients each. The primary outcome was MACE, defined as myocardial infarction (MI), ischemic stroke, or all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes were all-cause mortality, MI, atrial fibrillation (AF), and heart failure (HF) . 1
At 1 year, resmetirom was associated with lower risks of MACE (hazard ratio [HR], 0.50; 95% CI, 0.32-0.80; P = .003), all-cause mortality (HR, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.16-0.54; P <.001), and HF (HR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.42-0.99; P = .04). The 2 groups did not differ significantly in MI or AF. 1
At 2 years, the lower risks of MACE (HR, 0.61; 95% CI, 0.41-0.89; P = .01) and all-cause mortality (HR, 0.33; 95% CI, 0.20-0.55; P <.001) persisted. AF showed a nonsignificant trend favoring resmetirom (HR, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.41-1.07; P = .09), and MI rates remained similar. 1
Investigators described the findings as early real-world evidence that resmetirom may confer cardiovascular benefits beyond its established hepatic effects. The lower risks they observed emerged within the first year and persisted through 2 years of follow-up. 1
The analysis is retrospective and drew on electronic health records, so it can show associations but cannot establish causation. Propensity matching accounts only for variables recorded in the database, and residual confounding cannot be excluded. All-cause mortality was included in the MACE composite, while rates of MI did not differ between groups.1 Additionally, semaglutide has shown cardiovascular benefit in a randomized trial, but no randomized cardiovascular outcome data for resmetirom have been published. 2,4

articles.title_orig: Iran-Backed Militants Are Tightening the Screws on Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince
articles.title_zh: Iran-Backed Militants Are Tightening the Screws on Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Aviation Administration told U.S. airlines to exercise caution when flying in or around Saudi Arabia after deadly attacks claimed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, which have shut down the airport in the Saudi capital.
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, remains closed as of Monday after strikes that started last week. The attacks escalated Saturday, when a projectile struck a passenger terminal at the airport, officials said, killing at least 12 people and wounding more than 300.
Airlines suspended flights to the airport, some for the rest of the week.
The U.S., Australia and other countries advised citizens against travel to the region.
The FAA late Sunday said pilots should "exercise caution" in or around Saudi Arabia "due to safety-of-flight risks associated with ongoing military activities" and navigation systems. It said the threats could be a potential risk "to aircraft at all altitudes." The FAA's warning is in effect until Dec. 10.
Most U.S. airlines don't fly to Saudi Arabia, but the country's flights and passenger counts had climbed in recent years. The route between Riyadh to Jeddah in the country's west was the fifth-busiest in the world last year, according to aviation-data firm OAG.
Delta Air Lines had been scheduled to launch its first nonstop flight from Atlanta to Riyadh on Oct. 23 but the carrier on Monday said it would delay that service until March.

articles.title_orig: First Impressions: Dell XPS Googlebook and the Googlebook OS
articles.title_zh: First Impressions: Dell XPS Googlebook and the Googlebook OS
articles.content_orig:
Posted on October 12, 2026 Posted by John Scalzi 16 Comments
As someone who has, over the years, found himself deep in the Google ecosystem of hardware and services, I had been curious about the Googlebook concept for a while — whether it would be basically a fancy Chromebook, or if it would offer something more, and more useful , than that line of affordable but mostly limited laptops. When the Googlebook models were announced in September, I decided to go ahead and pre-order one: The Acer Googlebook 14.
It turns out, however, that apparently lots of people had the same idea as me. Best Buy sent me an email telling me that despite taking my pre-order money, the Acer was out of stock and they didn’t know when they would get more. I cancelled that order and went with the Dell XPS Googlebook instead, which, I think by virtue of being $100 more expensive than the Acer, was in stock. It arrived the day after I ordered it — and when, alas, I was away at New York Comic Con for a few days. I finally got a chance to set it up and play with it yesterday.
My first impressions: It’s pretty nice! Also, Google still has work to do on its shiny new operating system.
Hardware first: The XPS Googlebook is a really nice little laptop. It’s physically the smallest of the five Googlebooks available at launch (the other four coming from Acer, Asus, Hewlett-Packard and Lenovo). It’s clearly meant to be in the “ultrabook” category of laptop, which is to say, light and thin and not terribly concerned with ports (it comes with two USB-C ports and that’s it — not even a headphone jack). It’s also the only Googlebook at launch that does not come with an OLED screen, although the screen it has is perfectly nice and the blacks are certainly inky enough for government work.
All of the launch Googlebooks were required by Google to have certain minimum hardware: at least 16GB of RAM, high-speed processors, either by Intel or Qualcomm (the XPS comes with a Snapdragon X Elite), 512GB SSD, a metal, not plastic, chassis, backlit keyboard, and a touchscreen with a high refresh rate (120 Hz here). None of this comes cheap these days, and the initial set of Googlebooks are priced between $899 and $1299, with the XPS I got coming in at $999. This is more expensive than just about any Chromebook, more expensive than the new Macbook Neo, and on par with a newish Macbook Air.
The minimum requirements pay off, at least for the XPS. It feels really solid for such a small computer, and everything about it looks and feels nice. The keyboard has a nice snap to it and has almost no flex, the screen as mentioned is very good (and comes with an anti-glare coating, which is a feature I appreciate now that I have it), and while it has fans, which turned on while I was setting up the laptop, they are quiet and barely noticeable when they’re on, which so far has only been during that setup.
As mentioned the processor here is a Snapdragon chip rather than an Intel one, and that’s fine because Android (which the Googlebook OS is based on, and which, frankly, it’s mostly just a reskinned version of) is designed to run on ARM chips, which Snapdragon is. Everything runs quickly so far, and ARM chips are typically meant to be more efficient than x86 chips like Intel’s, although so far the battery life I’ve seen out of the XPS is good but not amazing.
The XPS has quirks — the keyboard is a modified Chromebook set-up, which means the Caps button is a “search” button first (you can make it a Caps button by holding down the shift button, which defeats the whole purpose of a caps button), and there’s a “Google” button on the bottom row which opens an app drawer or can be used to access the “magic pointer” (more on that later). Also, the speakers, while perfectly acceptable, make the chassis vibrate, particularly the trackpad, which is a not entirely pleasant feeling. The trackpad is mechanical, not haptic, and the click does take some pressure (it responds to taps perfectly well). The I/O situation as mentioned is sparse, but inasmuch as I already have a MacBook Air, which also only has two USB-C ports, I am already well-acquainted with the dongle life, and I have bluetooth headphones. I’m not going to give the XPS too much crap for that.
So as a piece of hardware, the XPS is solid. Now, how is the software — the Googlebook operating system and all the “AI” bells and whistles that Google has piled on top of it?
As a preface, I should note that I knew going into this that as an early adopter of this platform, I would essentially be a beta tester for it, since almost no 1.0 release of anything survives its first encounter with users out in the world. In the week since Googlebooks have hit the market there have already been updates to the OS to fix bugs and other flubs. So I’m okay with having a little patience in this shake-down cruise. That said, being patient doesn’t mean not pointing out the flaws that do currently exist.
One of those flaws is that at the moment the Googlebook is doing a crap job at one of its marquee features, namely, integration with Android phones, where one is supposed to be able to connect laptop and phone seamlessly, stream apps from the phone to the laptop, hand off work from one to the other, and drop files from one into the other painlessly. As a Pixel phone owner, this promised integration was a huge inducement to try out the Googlebook — I wanted what (presumably) iPhone users have with their Macs. It would, in fact, be really useful. And as a Pixel owner running Android 17, I am someone best positioned to get that integration right out of the box.
Except that the Googlebook keeps dropping its connection to my phone and not being able to find it after that, unless I restart both the phone and the Googlebook. It happens when I take my phone away from the laptop and/or close the laptop, breaking the connection between the two. A short disconnect doesn’t seem to be a problem; a longer one seems to flummox it entirely. I believe this is a known issue that’s being addressed, so that’s good. But it’s still annoying right now . I don’t want to have to keep resetting my laptop and phone to get the promised integration.
(I’ve also noticed that phone apps streamed onto the Googlebook can have choppy scrolling, although I don’t know if that’s a problem with the integration or an artifact of my occasionally-janky internet connection.)
That said, when the integration does work, it’s pretty neat, and I see it being really useful when I’m working on my laptop and need something from my phone, or want to access an app that I don’t have running natively on my computer. As mentioned already, the Googlebook OS is pretty much a reskinned version of Android 17, so all the apps that run on an Android phone should run just fine on the laptop (there are apps that apparently struggle on the Intel Googlebooks, but even there something like 97% of apps run perfectly well). During the setup, if you pair your Googlebook with your phone it will install the apps you have there over to the laptop, so you’ll be able to run them natively even if you can’t access your phone. But they are different instances of the app, so streaming an app might still come in handy.
So: Great in concept! Execution still needs work.
Google is going all in on “AI” integration on the Googlebooks, making sure that Gemini, its in-house “AI,” is only a click, button-mash or cursor wiggle away, the latter being the “magic pointer” feature. You can invoke Gemini and ask it about what’s on your screen, or have it smoosh two images you have into a single “AI”-ified picture and so on (the Googlebooks also come with an offer for an entire year of the “Pro” level of Gemini, which comes with five terabytes of cloud storage, which is arguably more useful). The point is, no matter where you go on the Googlebook OS, Gemini is right there, lurking, waiting for you to do something with it.

articles.title_orig: Bangladesh's Rooppur 1 achieves criticality
articles.title_zh: Bangladesh's Rooppur 1 achieves criticality
articles.content_orig:
The milestone was achieved three days after the go-ahead was given by the country's national atomic regulator.
A statement on the project's official Facebook account said: "This achievement is a significant step in Bangladesh's scientific and technological advancements and in the country's energy security. The Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant will play a crucial role in strengthening the country's energy security, diversifying electricity generation, and improving the development of low-carbon fuel systems.
"After achieving the required criteria, the test and safety verification process will be completed, and the reactor will be tested to operate at the minimum controllable capacity. If the subsequent tests are successfully completed, the national grid power supply operations will be advanced step by step."
The start-up of the unit followed talks in Moscow on Friday between Rosatom Director General Alexey Likhachev and Bangladesh's Science and Technology Minister Fakir Mahbub Anam.
According to Strana Rosatom , the in-house publication of Russia’s state nuclear corporation, the power start-up of the unit is scheduled for 20 November.
Before then there will be a series of tests and checks to ensure that all equipment and systems are working as designed. There will then be further tests and checks before the power start-up and as the power output is subsequently increased in stages.
Criticality means that the reactor has achieved a sustained nuclear chain reaction, with each fission event - when an atom of uranium in the fuel is split - releasing a sufficient number of neutrons to sustain an ongoing series of reactions.
In February 2011 Russia's Rosatom signed an agreement for two reactors to be built at Rooppur, about 160 kilometres from the capital Dhaka, for the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission. The initial contract for the project, worth USD12.65 billion, was signed in December 2015. The Bangladesh Atomic Regulatory Authority issued the first site licence for the Rooppur plant in June 2016, allowing preliminary site works, including geological surveys, to begin.
Construction of the first unit began in November 2017. Construction of the second unit began in July 2018. They have an initial life-cycle of 60 years, with a further 20-year extension possible.
The first batch of nuclear fuel was delivered to the site in October 2023 - the moment that the site got its status as a nuclear facility. In March last year, Rooppur unit 1's turbine installation was completed, as were hydraulic tests to check the primary circuit systems and equipment, followed by hot functional tests. An operating licence was issued by the Bangladesh Nuclear Regulatory Authority on 16 April this year. The process of loading 163 nuclear fuel assemblies into Bangladesh's first nuclear power plant reactor was completed in May.
Meanwhile, Rosatom announced on Monday 12 October, that JSC Rosatom Automated Control Systems had completed the installation of automated process control systems at the first and second power units of the Rooppur plant. Likhachev said: "The Rooppur NPP is not only the largest project of cooperation between the Russian Federation and the Republic of Bangladesh, but also our flagship in the use of modern automation and control technologies. This is Rosatom's first foreign plant to implement the Operator Information Support System. The system increases response times and reduces operating costs."

articles.title_orig: After Russian Diesel Deal, Trump Faces New Crisis Over Ukraine
articles.title_zh: After Russian Diesel Deal, Trump Faces New Crisis Over Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump has threatened to halt weapons supplies to Ukraine unless Kyiv ends its long-range strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
The White House made it clear to European officials over the weekend that a scheme allowing Ukraine’s allies to buy US arms and give them to Kyiv could be suspended.
Mr Trump is said to be angry at Volodymyr Zelensky ’s continued strikes on Russian oil refineries, and according to officials in Europe, the US administration has also threatened to withhold intelligence from Ukraine.
On Sunday, the US president announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, claiming the two sides had agreed not to attack one another’s energy infrastructure. He warned on Truth Social, his social media platform: “Do not break it!”
The announcement seemed to come as a surprise to both parties.
It followed Mr Trump’s announcement on Friday that he had agreed to buy “hundreds of thousands of tons” of diesel from Russia.
Hours after the energy ceasefire was announced, Russia attacked a power plant in Ukraine . Mr Zelensky said glide bombs and drones had hit a major facility in Kharkiv, the country’s second city.
On Monday, Mr Zelensky said: “If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond. If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people.”
Russia refused to say on Monday whether an agreement had been reached with Ukraine and the US.
“Contacts are continuing. As soon as we have anything to say on this matter, we will be sure to let you know,” Kremlin spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, said. Asked about Kyiv’s call for a 60-day complete ceasefire to enable it to hold elections, Peskov said: “We don’t want a ceasefire, we want long-term peace.”
Mr Trump has blamed the Russia-Ukraine war for high petrol and diesel prices, even though they have been exacerbated by America and Israel’s war with Iran.
European officials, who had received calls from US officials or been briefed on them, said the US had been lobbying ⁠European capitals and Kyiv to try to end the attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Threats from the Pentagon and State Department have included cutting off intelligence sharing and the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (Purl) mechanism for procuring US weapons for Ukraine.
One official told the Financial Times: “They are calling Kyiv, they are calling everyone [in Europe].” Another told CNN weapons purchases and intelligence sharing was “vital” to Ukraine, describing the threats from the US to end them as a “sad day” for Kyiv.
If acted on, the suspension of weapons supplies would have an immediate impact on the defence of Ukraine. Suspending weapons purchases through Purl would affect the supply of Patriot interceptor missiles, of which Ukraine is already experiencing a shortage.
The Trump administration temporarily suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine in March 2025 after a tense meeting between Mr Zelensky and Mr Trump in the Oval Office.
The White House declined to comment on the latest alleged threats.
Kaja Kallas , the EU’s foreign policy chief, said on Monday that the bloc would welcome a truce on striking energy infrastructure between Ukraine and Russia “when it holds”.
Speaking at a meeting of EU foreign ministers, she said: “We welcome the energy ceasefire when it holds. We haven’t yet seen that also Russia will stick to it.”
The EU’s top diplomat added that any truce needed to cover more than just oil refineries in the two countries, “where Ukraine has one and Russia has plenty, so it’s ... in the benefit of the Russians”.
Ukraine has been increasingly striking Russia’s refineries with long-range drones, crippling exports and contributing to an increase in energy prices. The strikes angered Mr Trump who declared: “He better damn well stop. I suggest they get a new leader who can ‌make a deal.”
Oil prices were lower on Monday morning after Mr Trump claimed he had brokered the ceasefire and eased sanctions on Russian oil. Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, was down 0.6 per cent at around $104 a barrel.
The FTSE 100 rose 0.5 per cent in early trading over the prospect of more oil being available in global markets. However, the picture was clouded by the Russian attacks on Ukrainian power plants and Houthi strikes on airports in Saudi Arabia .
Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “For now this looks more like an untested US proposal than a functioning ceasefire, particularly after a similar arrangement last month failed to endure.”

articles.title_orig: GOP ad buyer mixes up Portlands, spends money meant to help Maine Sen. Susan Collins in Oregon
articles.title_zh: GOP ad buyer mixes up Portlands, spends money meant to help Maine Sen. Susan Collins in Oregon
articles.content_orig:
The $25,000 ad, which accused the challenger to Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins of raising taxes, ran in Portland, Oregon.
For four days, a Republican super PAC ran its latest attack ad against Maine Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson, who is challenging incumbent Sen. Susan Collins in the November midterm elections.
The only problem was that the ad did not run in Portland, Maine. It ran in Portland, Oregon.
The Defending Main Street super PAC launched the ad, which ran last week as part of a GOP push to attack Jackson’s record on tax policy . Portland, Maine, was the intended target of the campaign spot, according to advertising data firm AdImpact, but it appears that roughly $25,000 worth of advertising ended up on the opposite coastline.
Titled “ So Many Taxes ,” the ad accused Jackson of supporting policies that raised costs for Mainers, an argument that likely fell on deaf ears across the rest of the country.
Data from the Google Ads Transparency Center shows that on digital platforms such as YouTube, the ad ended up playing primarily in the Portland, Oregon, metro area — roughly 2,500 miles from the Pine Tree State. While it is certainly true that none of the ad’s viewers are likely to cast a vote for Jackson come November, his opponent, Sen. Collins, is likely to find it difficult to reap any electoral rewards from tens of thousands of dollars spent in the West Coast market.
Collins is a member of the Republican Main Street Partnership, the conservative nonprofit parent organization of the super PAC that ran the ad. The ad was not directly authorized by the Collins campaign, and the campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the misplaced ad.
In a statement to MS NOW, Defending Main Street confirmed the mistake and blamed the ad’s misplacement on a vendor error.
“During a recent independent expenditure, our media vendor mistakenly placed approximately $25,000 in digital advertising in the Portland, Oregon media market instead of Portland, Maine,” the super PAC told MS NOW. “The vendor is refunding Defending Main Street the full amount of the misplaced spend. No donor funds will be lost as a result of the vendor’s error.”
AdImpact data shows the ad did make it to some voters in the Portland, Maine, media market via broadcast linear television, hitting about 675,000 impressions between Thursday and Sunday. By comparison, the digital ad on the opposite coast surpassed 1.5 million views Monday morning — and it cost the super PAC about twice as much.
Hannah Marr contributed to this report.
Adam Hudacek is an MS NOW desk associate in Washington, D.C. He covers agricultural policy, political culture and breaking news.

articles.title_zh: Meta releases its first frontier model, Muse Wonder
articles.content_orig:
Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now.
Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.
Meta’s Superintelligence Lab released a pair of new state-of-the-art models on Monday, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, representing the company’s first attempt at a frontier model.
Where Muse Spark aimed to be a lightweight model that could perform at low latency, the Wonder models are larger and said to be more capable, with higher benchmark scores and better results on complex tasks like coding.
According to Meta’s testing (presented in the model card ), Wonder and Wonder Full achieve comparable benchmark scores to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.
“Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” Meta’s blog post about the models reads.
That scale is reflected in the pricing: Accessed through the Meta Model API, Wonder will cost $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, making it roughly equivalent in cost to GPT-6 Sol or Opus 5.5.
Notably, Wonder Full will only be available to Muse Code subscribers and will not be served through the API. Both models will also be used to power the Muse agent.
In keeping with Meta’s interest in developing personal assistants that can perform tasks over a long period, the company placed particular emphasis on the new models’ ability to retain and synthesize information given by the user, a property Meta calls “active memory.”
To achieve better recall, Meta highlighted the MemoryBench benchmark , which challenges continual learning and memory construction frameworks. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder now scores higher on MemoryBench than Fable, Opus, or Astra.
“We put a tremendous amount of effort into making sure your model can remember what’s important to you over days, weeks, months, and beyond,” said research scientist Kavya Kopparapu in a video accompanying the launch.
The new models are the first frontier model release since Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang restructured Meta’s AI efforts in August of last year . Since then, Meta has released its lightweight Muse Spark model and Muse agent but has avoided the kind of state-of-the-art model releases OpenAI and Anthropic are known for.
According to the post, the models were trained at Meta’s Prometheus data center in central Ohio , which came online earlier this year.

articles.title_orig: Robert E. Hall wins Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
articles.title_zh: Robert E. Hall wins Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
articles.content_orig:
Berkeley’s world-class economics department is celebrating the Nobels won today by two scholars: Robert E. Hall, a 1964 graduate and early-career faculty member, and Michael Woodford, a visiting scholar in the 2025-26 academic year.
When the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences today announced the two winners of Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, the UC Berkeley economics community celebrated them as scholars who have achieved the heights of economic influence — and as colleagues with deep connections to the campus.
Robert E. Hall was an accomplished young scholar who earned his bachelor’s degree at UC Berkeley in 1964, and served on the economics faculty from 1967-1970 before moving to MIT and then to Stanford University. Michael Woodford, a scholar at Columbia University, was a deeply important teacher and mentor for some of Berkeley top young faculty economists even before coming to Berkeley as a visiting scholar last year.
Their remarkable careers, capped with the Nobel announcement yesterday, underscore the historic, extended influence of the Berkeley economics department in the 1960s — and affirm that Berkeley today is a robust center of contemporary economics, attracting some of the world’s most important scholars.
Six Berkeley economists have previously won the Nobel: David Card (2021), Oliver Williamson, (2009), George Akerlof (2001), Daniel McFadden (2000), John C. Harsanyi (1994) and Gérard Debreu (1983). Notably, James A. Robinson of the University of Chicago won the prize in 2024, honored in part for work on development economics that he had done from 1999-2004 while on the Berkeley faculty.
The Swedish Academy this year honored Hall and Woodford for what their scholarship tells policymakers about stabilizing the economy in turbulent times.
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” said John Hassler, chair of the academy’s Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences. “With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume.”
Hall, now 83, was born in Palo Alto. His selection crystallizes how profoundly important the 1960s were for Berkeley economics — and how the influence of that era resonates even today.
It was an extraordinary time, a gathering of titans. Debreau and Harsanyi were senior professors. Dale Jorgenson was on the faculty in that era; he’d won the John Bates Clark Medal, seen as the second highest honor for an economist, and was seen as a Nobel contender.
Williamson, McFadden and Peter Diamond were all young assistant professors, and Diamond would later win a Nobel while at MIT. Hall’s fellow student and Class of ’64 graduate, Thomas J. Sargent , would win the Nobel in 2011 for research on cause and effect in macroeconomics.
Even as an undergrad, Hall was making innovative contributions. He began research with Jorgenson that would lead to the seminal 1967 paper, “Tax Policy and Investment Behavior.”
The paper was “an instant classic,” said Michael Reich, who joined the Berkeley economics faculty in the fall of 1974 and now serves as Chair of the Center on Wage and Employment Dynamics. “It was required reading when I took a public finance class at Harvard in 1968, and it is still cited as a major contribution.”
Even after landing at Stanford, Hall maintained connections at Berkeley. For example, he delivered a talk at the centennial celebration of the economics department in 2002 and gave the department’s commencement address in 2006, when it was chaired by Ben Hermalin, now Berkeley’s executive vice chancellor and provost .
Woodford’s connection to Berkeley is more recent. Now 71, he arrived at Columbia by way of the University of Chicago, Yale Law School and MIT, where he earned his Ph.D.  For the 2025-26 academic year, Woodford was a visiting scholar at UC Berkeley.
“He is intellectually close to all of our macro group and also to the behavioral group,” said Stefano DellaVigna, the current chair of economics. “One way to think of his recent work in this area is that he builds on evidence from cognitive science and neuroscience on how people actually process information, and is able to show that getting that right really matters for understanding how people would process macroeconomic information, such as on inflation or economic growth.”
Woodford also spent time on the faculty at Princeton — that’s where he served as undergraduate thesis advisor to Emi Nakamura and Jón Steinsson in 2000 and 2001. Both are now on the Berkeley faculty.
Nakamura credits Woodford with encouraging her to focus on macroeconomics; she won the Clark Medal in 2019.
“The questions he asked about monetary policy were so interesting that it changed how I thought about economics as a whole,” Nakamura recounted. “As a thesis advisor, he was incredibly generous. I remember when I was working on my undergraduate thesis, struggling to understand the logic of one of the standard equations in the model, I sent him an email on December 24th, not expecting to hear back, of course. But he did write back — and really helped me understand what these equations were meant to represent.
“Later on in my career, I became increasingly aware of the impact that his work on monetary policy had on practical monetary policymaking around the world. My guess is that his research has had more practical impact on policymaking than almost any other economist. Anyone who visits a central bank almost anywhere in the world today is aware of this.”
After her studies, Nakamura joined the Columbia faculty, where Woodford became an important colleague.
“I remember a number of conversations I had with him at critical points in my own research, where he gave me some insight or encouragement that made a big difference,” she said. “Sometimes it was just a short conversation, but sometimes it was an insight that made all the difference. He was an amazing colleague to have.”

articles.title_orig: Trump blew past deadline to halt running taxpayer-funded campaign-style ads
articles.title_zh: Trump blew past deadline to halt running taxpayer-funded campaign-style ads
articles.content_orig:
A federal judge expressed alarm at how quickly the Trump administration moved to use taxpayer funds for midterm election advertisements following an Oval Office meeting between President Donald Trump and Republican operatives.
U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon issued a temporary restraining order Sunday to immediately stop the propaganda ads, a win for pro-democracy groups who argue they are an illegal misuse of funds appropriated by Congress.
The White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) was able to shift $20 million for the ads in a matter of hours, Rochon said in a 40-page opinion Monday explaining her decision.  The restraining order is necessary to ensure the government doesn’t just “reapportion funds from another source to continue running similar advertisements,” she wrote.
The New York Times reported earlier this month that Trump and his White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles, met with Republican strategists on August 7 to talk about the midterms and how to use money from a super PAC to support Republican candidates.
“During that meeting, President Trump reportedly expressed a desire to promote his administration and showed the strategists videos of himself, including footage later incorporated into one of the challenged advertisements,” Rochon wrote in her opinion.
Trump then tapped OMB Director Russell Vought to “find government funds to pay for the advertisements,” she added.
“Defendants do not deny that this meeting took place or dispute the reported substance of the various discussions, even though the Court expressly asked Defendants during the [temporary restraining order] conference on October 9, 2026 to address whether they disputed the reports of this meeting,” Rochon wrote.
Join 350,000 readers who rely on our daily and weekly newsletters for the latest in voting, elections and democracy.
Little over a month after the Oval Office meeting, the funds were made available through a U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) account for “commemorative events.” The process took just a few hours, the judge said.
“OMB initially apportioned $500,000 towards the commemorative category in November 2025,” Rochon wrote in her opinion. “On September 19, 2026, at 6:15 p.m., CBP submitted a request to OMB to reapportion funds that were appropriated by section 90004 of the Working Families Tax Cut Act within CBP’s ‘Operations and Support’ account. The CBP request sought to make an additional $20 million available for obligations under line 6043 for ‘commemorative events’ by reallocating funds from the following fiscal year. The request was approved by OMB that evening, less [than] two hours later, at 7:50 p.m.”
The next day, on Sept. 20, CBP made a $20 million purchase to LMD Agency for a “National Media Campaign.”
“The present apportionment was done quickly … and President Trump has publicly conveyed his belief that using appropriated taxpayer money is not only legal but a ‘standard thing to do,’” Rochon wrote.
In addition to not receiving “reasonable assurances” that the White House won’t find funds from another source to keep running the same or similar ads, Rochon said it’s unclear where the initial media buy stands.
A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) official told the court that the department hadn’t directed LMD to make “any additional” ad purchases past October 11.
“But this representation is somewhat unclear and leaves open whether LMD has already purchased ad placements scheduled to air after October 11, thereby continuing the alleged harm” to pro-democracy groups, Rochon said.
“Even if LMD has not purchased any further media buys for placement after October 11, Defendants have not shown that the ‘allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur,’” Rochon wrote.
The judge ordered the Trump administration to report back on its compliance with her order within 24 hours. Under the temporary restraining order , DHS can’t create, disseminate or air the challenged advertisements or enter into new contracts to do so.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo to be hospitalised on Tuesday ahead of lung surgery
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo to be hospitalised on Tuesday ahead of lung surgery
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV delivers the Angelus prayer in St. Peter's Square at the Vatican, Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. Gregorio Borgia/AP hide caption
Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday that he would have surgery this week to remove a "localized nodule" in his lung.
Leo said the nodule was found at a "very early stage" with doctors recommending surgery.
"Following their advice, I have therefore decided to undergo an operation to remove it," Leo said during his weekly Sunday noon blessing in St. Peter's Square.
The surgery will take place at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, which is the primary location for popes to receive medical attention.
"I thank you for your spiritual closeness and entrust myself to your prayers," Leo said to the crowds on Sunday. He later posted the message about his surgery on social media.
According to the American Cancer Society, a lung nodule is a small abnormal area , less than or equal to 3 cm, found during a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. These tests are often conducted as routine screenings for "trauma, heart disease, non-cancer related lung disease, or lung infection."
Dr. Panagis Galiatsatos, a pulmonary physician at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, said lung nodules are common in older adults.
"The majority of lung nodules are benign," Galiatsatos said. "I usually call them the lungs' wrinkles"
When they're discovered, doctors will test them to determine whether there is cause for concern.
"If they're now discussing that they need to remove the lung nodule, one of his tests must have crossed their threshold … and the suspicion and concern for cancer became a little bit higher," Galiatsatos said. "So that's why he's undergoing this surgery."
Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni said in a statement that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of this week and the estimated post-operative recovery time will be about one week."
Leo's next major international trip is scheduled for early November to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear if the surgery would affect his itinerary.
During his papacy, Leo has been outspoken about peace throughout the world. He spent part of his Sunday address renewing calls for peace in Ukraine.
"I make a heartfelt appeal to the parties to the conflict to allow the safe transport of grain across the Black Sea," Leo said. "The daily bread of millions of people cannot be held hostage by war."
On Saturday, the Pope also called for the death penalty to be abolished, saying on X that it is "inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person."
"The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption," Leo said.

articles.title_orig: Mamdani orders review of NYPD's use-of-force policies as progressives call for greater change
articles.title_zh: Mamdani orders review of NYPD's use-of-force policies as progressives call for greater change
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK CITY (WABC) -- Mayor Zohran Mamdani has directed the NYPD to conduct its first comprehensive review of use-of-force policies and practices in a decade and announced a series of reforms aimed at strengthening accountability for officers accused of serious misconduct.
The review, which will take place over the coming months, comes as the administration faces mounting pressure from some supporters to follow through on campaign promises related to policing, including calls to dismantle the NYPD's Strategic Response Group. The mayor also said he has no plans to remove Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch.
According to the mayor's office, the review will include a community engagement process and examine how the department's use-of-force policies are applied and whether changes are needed. The administration said it is the first such review in 10 years.
The changes come after scrutiny of an NYPD officer's retirement following the fatal police shooting of Win Rozario , a 19-year-old who was suffering an apparent psychiatric episode when officers were called to his Ozone Park, Queens, home in May 2024. Rozario was shot and killed after he lunged at officers with a pair of scissors.
The officers were cleared by the state attorney general, but the Civilian Complaint Review Board later concluded that they used excessive force.
One of the officers, Salvatore Alongi, was allowed to retire before he could face an administrative trial because the NYPD failed to inform the review board. NYPD Commissioner Tisch acknowledged the failure as an oversight.
Mamdani said the reforms are intended to increase accountability within the department.
"When the government uses force against a New Yorker, the standard for accountability must be at its highest," he said. "Every New Yorker deserves to know that force will be used lawfully, carefully and only when necessary."
In addition to reviewing use-of-force guidelines, the department will strengthen pending retirement notifications. The city will increase funding for the inspector general that monitors the NYPD, and the department will standardize public disclosure protocols for police-involved incidents.
Ninety percent of New York City police officers go their entire careers without a single substantiated civilian complaint. The police union said that number would be even higher if the Civilian Complaint Review Board took what it called an "unbiased" approach.
"There should be no review of the NYPD's use of force policies," said the PBA president, "without a corresponding review of the blatantly biased and unjust way those policies are interpreted by the Civilian Complaint Review Board."
Critics, however, said the mayor's reforms do not go far enough.
Loyda Colon, executive director of the Justice Committee, a support network for victims of police violence, said a broader overhaul is needed.
"Does there need to be a full overhaul of the NYPD discipline process? Yes, but that's also after the fact. There's good intent here, but this is far from enough."

articles.title_orig: Trump Gives Putin a Hand in Russia’s Economic War With Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Trump Gives Putin a Hand in Russia’s Economic War With Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Monday defended last week's decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel fuel exports after the announcement drew bipartisan criticism .
Trump, in a Truth Social post , accused the media of hypocrisy for allegedly refusing to cover past purchases of Russian energy by the European Union.
"The European Union paid Russia 250 Billion Dollars for Energy, and the Fake News Media doesn't want to get near that story," Trump wrote.
While the president did not specify, his figure roughly tracks with some estimates of how much the EU has spent importing fossil fuels from Russia since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The European Commission has launched a plan to phase out its dependence on Russian energy.
"I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!" Trump wrote in the social media post.
Lawmakers from both parties raised concerns about Trump's decision to let Russia supply some diesel to the U.S. and global markets for the next six months.
The plan received pushback from multiple congressional Republicans who have urged Trump not to lift the U.S. ban on energy imports from Russia until its president, Vladimir Putin , ends the war against Ukraine.
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," a group of seven senators, including four Republicans, said in a joint statement on Sunday.
Other Republicans have also raised issues with Trump's deal.
"While I understand the desire to bring down diesel prices, I am concerned the lifting of sanctions on Russian oil will only fund the Kremlin's war machine—emboldening more violence and destruction, as we have seen in recent days," Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas, said Friday.
Trump, whose party is staring down a potentially tough midterm election that has coincided with widespread economic dissatisfaction, says the plan he coordinated with Putin will help bring down sky-high diesel prices. Some analysts say the policy won't make much of a dent , however.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that the U.S. easing sanctions on Moscow "plays into Russia's hands."

articles.title_orig: Duo Share Nobel in Economics for Work on Steering Through Booms and Busts
articles.title_zh: Duo Share Nobel in Economics for Work on Steering Through Booms and Busts
articles.content_orig:
English English (pdf) Swedish Swedish (pdf)
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has decided to award the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2026 to
Robert E. Hall Stanford University, CA, USA.
Michael Woodford Columbia University, New York, USA.
“for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”
This year’s laureates in the economic sciences, Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford, have developed new macroeconomic models that have significantly improved our ability to implement effective stabilisation policy. On the basis of these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the economy’s peaks and troughs.
The economy is characterised by alternating downturns and upturns. Ever since the economist John Maynard Keynes launched his theories almost a century ago, stabilisation policy has been important for tackling these fluctuations. During recessions, the economy is boosted by reducing interest rates and increasing the budget deficit, while the opposite should be done to slow a booming economy.
However, during the oil crises of the 1970s, it seemed that the Keynesian models that govern when and how measures should be implemented no longer worked. They did not reduce unemployment, but led to uncontrolled inflation instead. The West experienced a decade of low growth, high unemployment and high inflation. Many people believed that stabilisation policy had done more harm than good and that it should be retired.
Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford are awarded this year’s prize in economic sciences for demonstrating how economic models could be reconstructed to revitalise stabilisation policy. Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation. This encompasses an understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions.
A central component in these models is that households and businesses are forward looking when making decisions about savings or product prices. When governments and central banks communicate their plans for economic policy, they can influence this view of the future and move the economy in the right direction. Since the new models’ introduction, they have been extremely helpful in dealing with the economic downturns that have affected us.
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” says John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.
The illustrations are free to use for non-commercial purposes. Attribute ”© Johan Jarnestad/The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences”

The Academy takes special responsibility for the natural sciences and mathematics, but endeavours to promote the exchange of ideas between various disciplines.
