articles.title_orig: Apple 'Welcome Home' Launch: Everything to Expect Tomorrow
articles.title_zh: Apple 'Welcome Home' Launch: Everything to Expect Tomorrow
articles.content_orig:
Apple's "Welcome Home" product launch is happening tomorrow. As the name suggests, Apple is going to debut new home accessories, including the long-rumored home hub.
Below, we've listed all the rumors we know about the three devices Apple is set to introduce.
Apple's home hub, which will be called HomeView , is a multi-function device designed for all of a home's occupants. It's built around Siri AI, and will have an A18 chip and 8GB of RAM.
Here's what rumors suggest it'll be able to do:
The hub will be able to do anything you might want a home assistant device to do, from giving the next steps of a recipe to suggesting dinner ideas and creating a shopping list. It will rely heavily on ‌Siri‌ AI for voice-based input, but it will also have a 6-inch touch display.
The display is square with bezels around the edges, and there are two models. One version can be mounted on the wall, and the other is attached to a half-dome speaker base with a flexible arm for adjusting tilt. The hub isn't expected to have its own App Store , but it will support Apple apps such as Safari, News, Music, Reminders, Calendar, Weather, Messages, FaceTime , Photos , and Mail.
There will be a presence sensor and a camera in the hub, and it will use a variation of Face ID to determine who is nearby to show customized content. It will display information from a linked iPhone, like email messages, but only after authenticating. The sensors in the hub will be usable in HomeKit scenes and automations, so you can use it to trigger lights and other devices when a person walks into the room.
The interface will be heavily widget-based so you can see information at a glance, and it's likely going to look similar to StandBy mode on the iPhone. You will be able to choose your preferred clock face or idle state, along with a home screen of widget options that you can tap to open a full app. If you have multiple hubs, they'll link together for features like multi-room music and intercom functionality. Rumors suggest that it will have better sound quality than the HomePod mini .
There isn't going to be a built-in battery, and the hub will need to be connected to power via an included USB-C port. The speaker-equipped version is expected in multiple colors, including gray, silver, starlight, and rose. The wall-mounted version will be available in silver and gray.
Rumors suggest the hub could be priced somewhere around $350.
Apple isn't updating the design of the Apple TV , so expect the new model to be the same boring black box. What's changing is entirely inside.
The ‌Apple TV‌ 4K is going to get a lot more powerful so it can support ‌Siri‌ AI, offering many of the same ‌Siri‌ features that are available on iPhone and iPad in iOS and iPadOS 27 .
We're expecting an A19 with 8GB of RAM, along with Apple's N1 networking chip for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread. The A19 will bring a major upgrade in performance, both for ‌Siri‌ and for gaming. It has ray tracing, mesh shading, and other features that will improve gameplay graphics.
There will be a new ‌Siri‌ Remote with an included speaker to make it easier to find, and we've seen some signs that Apple is working on its own gaming controller under the Beats brand , but there's no word on whether it's ready to launch.
Apple will likely emphasize ‌Siri‌ AI and gaming capabilities when introducing the ‌Apple TV‌. Apple raised the price of the current ‌Apple TV‌ to $199 in June, and the new model will be at least that expensive with the processor and RAM upgrades.
Like the ‌Apple TV‌ 4K, the ‌HomePod mini‌ isn't going to get a new design, but it will have internal upgrades that make it more capable. It's going to get an upgraded S10 chip, second-generation UWB for features like Handoff, and the N1 networking chip with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.
You'll need a nearby AI-capable device for ‌Siri‌ AI processing because the HomePod probably won't be able to handle much on-device, but smarter ‌Siri‌ should make for a better experience. ‌Siri‌ AI on ‌HomePod mini‌ will have the context of ‌Siri‌ interactions on other devices, and it's likely conversations will be saved to a connected iPhone's ‌Siri‌ app.
‌Siri‌ AI can answer follow-up questions, handle multi-request queries, and access information from your apps. It'll be similar to having ChatGPT or Claude on a speaker. Though design updates aren't expected, the ‌HomePod mini‌ will get new colors. We're expecting white, blue, black, sage, and pink.
‌HomePod mini‌ pricing went up from $99 to $129 in June 2026, and the new model will likely be priced at $129 too.
Apple worked with LG to make an LG-branded wired video doorbell, thermostat, smart deadbolt lock, temperature sensor, indoor security camera, outdoor security camera, and floodlight camera that will work with the home hub and the ‌HomeKit‌ platform.
The accessories are part of an "Apple Home Collection" that will be marketed alongside the HomeView. They won't be ready until later this year at the earliest, but Apple could show them off during the announcement.
There's no keynote event for the "Welcome Home" product debut, so Apple is probably going to release a video and an accompanying set of press releases. There's an NYC media event that's going to take place at 9:00 a.m. Eastern Time on Tuesday, October 13, and that could be when all of the announcements happen.
The NYC event will let members of the media get some hands-on time with the new devices to share first impressions.
Apple could begin accepting pre-orders just after the new devices launch. The ‌HomePod mini‌ and the ‌Apple TV‌ 4K are going to launch on Friday, October 30.
The HomeView won't be available right away and is expected to ship to customers in mid-November .

articles.title_orig: You Can Now Set Up Your iPhone Duo Pre-Order - Do It Before Friday
articles.title_zh: You Can Now Set Up Your iPhone Duo Pre-Order - Do It Before Friday
articles.content_orig:
Apple has opened its "Get Ready" service for iPhone Duo pre-orders, allowing customers to pre-select a variety of options to streamline the process of ordering and have a better chance of grabbing one on launch day.
The iPhone Duo launches on October 23, while pre-orders go live on October 16 at 5 a.m. Pacific Time or 8 a.m. Eastern Time. Rather than turn up on the day, however, Apple encourages customers to take action before then and increase the chances of securing their preferred model on day one of sales.
Get Ready is an option available on Apple's online store and in its Apple Store app , and it lets you select a preferred color and capacity ahead of time. It also lets you confirm your carrier status, choose your accessories, pick an AppleCare+ plan, select a trade-in, add a payment method, and set a shipping and billing address.
Get Ready is really helpful because when pre-orders go live, it allows you to essentially perform a one-tap order. That's a real advantage when it comes to iPhone Duo, given that supplies are expected to be limited.
It's been said before about other iPhones, but pre-orders of the iPhone Duo really could sell out within minutes – there have been multiple reports of production issues leading to supply constraints, and users who have completed Get Ready will be able to submit orders faster.
So if you're set on being one of the first to get hold of Apple's debut foldable, make sure to visit Apple's website or Apple Store app and complete the Get Ready process now.

articles.title_orig: World’s tiniest flowering plant could feed deep space astronauts
articles.title_zh: World’s tiniest flowering plant could feed deep space astronauts
articles.content_orig:
Duckweed on end of pencil. (University of Nottingham via SWNS)
The world’s smallest flowering plant would be an “ideal” food crop for future space missions , according to new research.
Duckweeds measure just a few millimeters across, but scientists say they could feed astronauts exploring deep space — as well as providing a potential source of food and protein on Earth.
Researchers at the University of Nottingham conducted gene expression analysis and cutting-edge microscopy on duckweeds.
Their findings, published in the journal Current Biology , show that they retain the same basic building blocks found in the shoots of larger plants.
But those structures have been “dramatically compressed” and fused together.
(Photo by Samiran Biswas via Pexels)
Study leader Anthony Bishopp says miniaturization is a “remarkable phenomenon” found throughout the natural world, from tiny animals to miniature plants.
He said: “Duckweeds are extraordinary flowering plants that can measure just a few millimeters across, yet their relatives include some of the largest herbaceous plants.
“We were interested to find out how a complete plant body plan can be packed into such a tiny space.
“While miniaturization in animals is often associated with the loss of organs or body structures, we have revealed that duckweeds have taken a different route.
“What surprised us is that, when we looked closely, the basic organization of the shoot was still there.
“Rather than throwing away parts of the blueprint, duckweed appears to have compressed and fused its components into an incredibly compact plant.
(Photo by Petr Ganaj via Pexels)
“That gives us a new way of thinking about how plants can evolve to become so small.”
Bishopp said duckweed research is advancing rapidly, driven by growing interest in the tiny plants as a potential source of food and novel protein on Earth, as well as a possible crop for future space missions.
He added: “Unlike most of the crops we grow today, which have been shaped by thousands of years of domestication and selective breeding, the potential of duckweed remains largely unexplored.
“Even the basic architecture of the duckweed plant has remained something of a mystery.
“Understanding how its body is organized provides an essential framework for understanding how duckweed grows, develops and functions — and ultimately how its potential might be improved.”
Study co-author Alex Ware said: “Duckweeds are astonishingly small, so it is tempting to think of them as either primitive plants or simply as having lost parts, but this is not the case.”
Ware added: “Our research adds to growing evidence from across the research community about this plant and will help efforts to turn them into a future crop.”

articles.title_orig: US attorney warns Chinese espionage is 'extremely pervasive,' says Beijing 'playing the long game'
articles.title_zh: US attorney warns Chinese espionage is 'extremely pervasive,' says Beijing 'playing the long game'
articles.content_orig:
First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli told Fox News Digital that Chinese government-backed espionage is "extremely pervasive" in the U.S.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said Chinese espionage is "extremely pervasive" in the U.S. following the arrest of an alleged Chinese agent in Los Angeles this month.
Essayli told Fox News Digital in an interview that his office has pressed charges against several alleged Chinese spies in recent months, saying Beijing is brazen in its attempts to build their access inside the U.S.
"I think it's extremely pervasive," Essayli said of Chinese spying. " China is one of our biggest adversaries, and they're committed to advancing their interests. And they're playing the long game, and so they are willing to put a lot of resources into developing sources, recruiting people within the U.S. to advance their interests.
CHINA EXPERT WARNS BEIJING WANTS AMERICANS — NOT THE CCP — TO SPREAD ITS MESSAGE
First Assistant United States Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli speaks as U.S. and Canadian law enforcement officials announce federal charges and arrests of alleged members of a transnational organized crime group at FBI offices in Los Angeles, Calif., on July 7, 2026. (REUTERS)
"They're willing to steal our technology; they're willing to engage in espionage here. So, there's no limit to what China is willing to do. It is a huge, huge concern. We have to be vigilant, and we have to disrupt these operations on our soil," Essayli said. "We have to protect our sovereignty."
"If you look at just the cases we brought this year, just in my office, I mean, you had cases where the woman from Irvine was engaged in espionage against the Taiwanese president's family member . I had a guy last week we arrested, he sold more than $300 million in SI chips, formerly known as AI chips, to China," he continued. "You had a mayor of a local city that we charged for serving as an unregistered agent of China as well, pushing out their propaganda and taking orders from China."
FORMER CALIFORNIA MAYOR ADMITS TO SECRETLY WORKING FOR CHINA, SPREADING BEIJING PROPAGANDA IN US
This photo provided by the Federal Bureau of Investigation shows Wanying Zhang being arrested Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026, in Los Angeles. (Federal Bureau of Investigation via AP)
"So, it's extremely pervasive. It's a huge problem, but the FBI is on it," he said. "They have entire squads dedicated to combating this, and we're committed here at the U.S. Attorney's Office to supporting those investigations and bringing criminal charges to disrupt these operations."
Wanying Zhang, 34, of Irvine, was arrested earlier this month for allegedly working with an associate to photograph and record the family outside their Seattle-area home, according to a criminal complaint obtained by Fox News Digital.
CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN
Authorities nabbed Zhang, who goes by "Heather" in the U.S., at the Los Angeles airport as she attempted to board a plane to China.
This undated photo released by the U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, shows Wanying Zhang. (U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California via AP)
Essayli said FBI Los Angeles agents arrested Zhang on a federal charge of acting as an unregistered agent of the People’s Republic of China.
CALIFORNIA MAYOR ACCUSED OF SECRETLY WORKING FOR CHINA, SPREADING PROPAGANDA WHILE IN OFFICE: FEDS
She allegedly traveled to Seattle in 2025 at the direction of Chinese officials and sent them photos, videos and license plate information.
"She coordinated the trip with an associate and used tradecraft to avoid detection," Essayli wrote. "She never notified the attorney general she was acting for a foreign government, a federal offense."

articles.title_orig: Starbucks puts an end to acquisition reports
articles.title_zh: Starbucks puts an end to acquisition reports
articles.content_orig:
Starbucks on Monday denied it is considering acquiring Chipotle Mexican Grill in what would be the biggest-ever restaurant takeover.
"Starbucks is not buying Chipotle," a Starbucks spokesperson told CNBC's Jim Cramer.
Chipotle's stock was down nearly 4% in morning trading Monday following the statement, while Starbucks shares were 1% higher.
The coffee giant's denial comes after days of rumors about a potential megadeal between the two restaurant companies.
On Thursday, the Financial Times reported that Starbucks had been working with advisors on a Chipotle takeover proposal in recent months. The newspaper cited people familiar with the matter.
Earlier in October, Semafor reported that Chipotle had hired advisors to defend against activist investors or an unwanted takeover bid. The fast-casual chain is trying to recover from a rocky 2025 , when traffic to its restaurants fell. Chipotle shares are down about 20% over the last year, making it a cheaper target.
The deal rumors sent shares of Chipotle higher, while Starbucks stock fell on the reports.
Chipotle investors were looking forward to a potential reunion with Brian Niccol, who previously led Chipotle and is now CEO of Starbucks. But Starbucks shareholders were largely concerned about an expensive distraction while the coffee chain is in the middle of its own turnaround.

articles.title_orig: Blindsided again by Trump, Europe scrambles to rally behind Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Blindsided again by Trump, Europe scrambles to rally behind Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Europe is once again trying to save face after US President Donald Trump blindsided the continent by striking a tailored deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, to release thousands of tonnes of diesel that had until now been sanctioned.
The news alarmed Ukraine and its European allies, who have long been wary of Trump's unpredictable diplomacy and his understanding of what a just and lasting peace means.
Tensions between the two sides of the Atlantic have never fully receded since February last year, when Trump unexpectedly called Putin and launched negotiations to end the war without consulting any European leader in advance.
That was the start of a series of unexpected developments that have rattled Europe and upended its long-held assumptions about the post-war international order. These include a hastily organised Trump-Putin summit in Alaska, a leaked 28-point plan heavily favourable to Moscow and a sanctions waiver for Russian crude oil.
The diesel deal, announced on Friday on Truth Social, added yet another chapter.
Trump then resorted to a familiar pattern: public attacks against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's legitimacy and calls for fresh elections. Ukraine's constitution bars elections in wartime, a point that Zelenskyy tends to remind Trump.
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does," Trump said to Moscow's applause.
As in previous episodes, Europe finds itself scrambling to close ranks, rally behind Ukraine and make clear that, regardless of what the White House does and says, this side of the Atlantic will stay the agreed course.
"I think we need to be collectively serious. Today, I believe, we have no factual reason to change our position," French President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said emulating the Trump-Putin diesel deal was "out of the question" for Europe, despite rising energy prices.
"Russia will only negotiate seriously under pressure, and that is why we are sticking to our sanctions against Russia," Merz told reporters.
A similar message echoed through Luxembourg as EU foreign ministers met and insisted that the pressure campaign on Moscow would continue unabated. Some openly decried the diesel deal, calling it regrettable and concerning.
Foreign ministers also approved a record-breaking addition of 1,600 names to the sanctions list, half of them linked to the production of ballistic missiles that fall on Ukraine. The contrast between the EU and the US could hardly have been starker.
"We showed unity today on these (1,600) listings," High Representative Kaja Kallas said at the end of the meeting.
"But, of course, it would be much stronger if we had acted together with the US. Our message to the United States is that only pressure works with Russia."
Although the Trump-Putin deal fits a familiar pattern of erratic diplomacy that sidelines European interests, its grim context sets it apart.
The diesel deal comes at a time when Russia is rapidly escalating its attacks against Ukraine, killing scores of civilians and wrecking the levers that sustain the local economy, including power stations, data centres, warehouses and railways.
Russia's blockade in the Black Sea has left Ukrainian farmers unable to send tonnes of grain to their global clients and deprived the state of an essential revenue source.
As economic activity stagnates and material costs pile up, the EU is realising its multibillion-euro lines of support will fall short sometime next year. With the US out of the picture, the burden is set to fall on the European pocket.
The prospect of Russia selling diesel that had until now been sanctioned and making extra money to finance the bombs that rain down on Ukraine is particularly difficult to stomach for Kyiv and its allies. It also raises serious questions about how much the US can be trusted to provide security guarantees for the post-war scenario.
And yet, Europe's collective assessment remains that there is still more to lose than to gain from breaking away from the Americans.
"What we need to do is refocus and redouble our efforts in keeping pressure on Russia," Ireland's Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said on Monday.
"Our priority has to be to maintain that pressure, but also to maintain our channels with the US, because this is not going to be achievable without the support of the US."
Just as news of the diesel deal broke, senior officials from Ukraine, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the European Commission and NATO were in Miami, Florida, for a round of talks hosted by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump's special envoys.
The meeting was the first of its kind since the outbreak of the US-Iran war, which has absorbed the White House's foreign policy and relegated Ukraine to the second row.
"We will continue to engage with our partners and also with the US in bringing this war to a close, and the latest example of this has been the talks on Friday in Miami," the Commission's chief spokesperson said, describing the meeting as a "positive step".
Europe initially struggled to secure a seat at the negotiating table as Trump and Putin marched ahead with their private calls. It took months after European countries established the “Coalition of the Willing” for them to be brought into the US-led negotiating process.
The statements from Brussels confirm that retaining a seat at the table where Ukraine’s future as a sovereign state and Europe’s security architecture will be decided takes precedence over any diplomatic slight, however pointed or public.
Zelenskyy, whose country is already suffering blackouts ahead of a winter expected to be the harshest yet of the war, agrees that the transatlantic alliance must prevail, notwithstanding the deals that might be cut behind its back.
"An energy ceasefire and other steps to reduce escalation and guarantee security are truly needed here – in reality, not just on Truth Social," Zelenskyy said.
"We need to end Russia's war. We need to guarantee security. We need to stand together. Europe and the United States."

articles.title_orig: Let’s Break Down Kelly Clarkson’s Brooklyn Toy Store Beef
articles.title_zh: Let’s Break Down Kelly Clarkson’s Brooklyn Toy Store Beef
articles.content_orig:
Things you buy through our links may earn Vox Media a commission
Did Kelly Clarkson get Pretty Woman ’d by a snooty toy store in Brooklyn? Or did she pull a full “Do you know who I am?” on a small, local business in front of the entire internet? For two days, Clarkson has been embroiled in an online back-and-forth with Art of Play, a novelty shop in the tony neighborhood of Brooklyn Heights which is owned by twin brothers Dan and Dave Buck and Adam Rubin . Clarkson says she inquired about a pricy item in the shop and the employees implied she could not afford the piece. Art of Play says the item Clarkson was asking about wasn’t for sale at all, but they tried to accommodate her request as best they could.
The brouhaha began on Saturday, when Clarkson tweeted that she’d just driven “all the way to Brooklyn” to check out Art of Play, which she said “looked really rad,” and there were even a few specific things she had her eye on to purchase. Unfortunately, she said, the person helping her looked at her “as if I couldn’t afford it” and offered to find something comparable. “Wow, dude,” Clarkson wrote. “You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale.” Big mistake! Huge!
Not long afterwards, the store responded with their own statement, saying that Clarkson “inquired about buying ’Molly,’ a one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird automaton who plays an important role in the magic shows we host here.” According to the store, Molly is “permanently attached to the wall and isn’t for sale.” The statement continued, “Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by 8 million people who have never visited our store.”
This was not the end of the back-and-forth, however. Clarkson then returned to X and her Instagram stories with a second statement, accusing the store of outright lying, and including a photo of the bird with an attached $15,000 price tag. “So the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn’t happen as you elevator eyed me saying in a condescending tone ‘yes, it’s for sale but it costs 15,000 dollars so if you’d like me to find something comparable for you I can,’” Clarkson wrote.
Art of Play then issued a “clarification,” stating that while Molly is permanently attached to the wall, the Seattle-based artist who created the automaton has another, nearly identical bird and, “He told us he would be willing to part with Molly’s twin for $15,000.” The store said they then offered Clarkson “a different singing bird automaton, made by a traditional clockmaking shop in Germany, that she could have taken home with her that day. It costs about $2,000.” However, the shop stated, “She did not stick around long enough to see it.”
In the meantime, Art of Play has been reposting supportive messages from customers, influencers, and friends to its Instagram Stories and has pinned a post from September titled, “Our favorite items not for sale…” The post includes a picture of the bird automaton, but also text reading, “While the objects on our shelves have a price, what happens when you play with them is free.”
So far, neither party has backed down nor issued a real apology — leaving it to the internet to decide which of the people arguing over a $15,000 singing bird is the real victim here.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk quietly becomes biggest known donor in midterm contests as he tries to save Republicans
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk quietly becomes biggest known donor in midterm contests as he tries to save Republicans
articles.content_orig:
by NATALIA MITTELSTADT | The National News Desk
WASHINGTON (TNND) — Elon Musk has given $276 million to Republican super PACs over the last three months for the midterm elections, making him the largest known donor this cycle.
Musk, a trillionaire, has contributed $366 million in total thus far, a spokesperson for his America PAC told The Hill .
From July to September, Musk gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC backing GOP Senate candidates, and $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, which gives support to GOP House candidates.
Musk launched his America PAC during the 2024 election, which has received more than $76 million. The SpaceX CEO also gave $10 million to the Lone Star Liberty PAC supporting Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, $10 million to the Republican Governors Association, and $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association.
The Congressional Leadership Fund, the Republican Governors Association, the Republican Attorneys General Association, the Lone Star Liberty PAC, and the Senate Leadership Fund didn't respond to The Hill's requests for comment.
After donating hundreds of millions of dollars to support President Trump's 2024 campaign, Musk was brought on to the administration last year to lead the Department of Government Efficiency. After leaving the White House in May 2025 and a public fallout with Trump, Musk stayed quiet for months when it came to politics.
This past May, Musk said he planned to spend “a lot less” on politics, then said in July that he “got carried away” and “a little too involved in politics.” Also in July, Musk authorized his America PAC to spend $100-$120 million for a new field program focused on conservative voter turnout in the midterms .
Trump and Musk have since rekindled their alliance, with the president awarding the Tesla CEO the National Medal of Science last week.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
U.S. stocks traded mixed on Monday, with the Dow rising more than 250 points while the Nasdaq Composite fell amid pressure on semiconductor stocks.
Salesforce shares climbed after Bank of America upgraded the stock to 'Buy' from 'Underperform' and raised its price target to $285 from $160.
Micron and SanDisk declined amid concerns about growing competition from China's CXMT.
U.S. equities traded mixed on Monday, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average rising more than 200 points while the Nasdaq Composite slipped as Micron Technology (MU) and other chip stocks tumbled on concerns about competition from China's CXMT.
Adding to market pressure, oil prices climbed amid renewed Russia-Ukraine tensions. Investors were also looking ahead to bank earnings, upcoming inflation data, and a Friday speech by Kevin Warsh this week.

The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) edged 0.04% lower at the time of writing, the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) gained 0.40%, and the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) slipped as much as 0.60%. Retail sentiment around QQQ on Stocktwits dropped to 'bullish' from 'extremely bullish' over the past day.
The Dow received support from Salesforce (CRM), which rose after Bank of America (BofA) gave it a double upgrade to 'Buy' from 'Underperform' and raised its price target to $285 from $160.
The firm cited improving prospects for Salesforce's artificial intelligence strategy and stated that large companies are unlikely to abandon established software platforms that house their business data and workflows.
The Nasdaq, on the other hand, faced pressure from semiconductor stocks. Concerns that CXMT could pose bigger competition in memory chips weighed on Micron (MU), SanDisk (SNDK) and other chip companies in the sector. SNDK stock tumbled 5.6% in midday trade, while MU stock fell by around 3%.
Wells Fargo's double downgrade on Adobe (ADBE) also did not help. The firm downgraded the software maker to 'Underweight' from 'Equal Weight' and lowered its price target to $225 from $270. It cited concerns about slowing organic growth and the challenge of meeting Adobe's full-year targets.
The S&P 500, which covers a broader cross-section of large U.S. companies, held relatively steady as gains in some stocks offset losses elsewhere. eBay (EBAY) was among the top gainers, alongside names like Meta Platforms (META) and Biogen (BIIB).
EBAY stock was also among the top-trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing, gaining as much as 5.5% in the midday trade and marking an over-four-month high. The rally came after Morgan Stanley named the company its top pick in the internet sector. Retail sentiment around the shares on the platform trended in 'bullish' territory over the past day.
Cerebras Systems (CBRS) was among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits and one of the market's biggest losers, falling 9.6% in midday trade, extending its decline after a report last week suggested OpenAI was using Nvidia (NVDA) chips rather than Cerebras' hardware for a feature of its latest AI model. CBRS stock hit a record low of $147.77, leaving it at less than half of its $350 IPO price.
Oil prices added another source of uncertainty for investors. West Texas Intermediate crude futures expiring in November rose over 2% to around more than $93 a barrel in midday trade, while Brent crude futures expiring in December also gained around 2% to trade near $107 a barrel.
The most recent uptick comes after renewed attacks on energy infrastructure and questions over an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine announced by President Donald Trump over the weekend. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had already violated the agreement, raising doubts about whether the arrangement would ease risks to energy supplies.
The United States Oil Fund (USO) rose around 2.3% in midday trade on Monday. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the ETF trended in 'bearish' territory over the past day.
Major U.S. banks are also due to report quarterly results this week, while the September consumer price index will offer a fresh reading on inflation and could influence expectations for the Federal Reserve's next policy decision. Kevin Warsh is scheduled to speak later in the week at an International Monetary Fund and World Bank event in Bangkok.

articles.title_orig: It’s a Real Shame the OnePlus 16 Is Launching Only in China
articles.title_zh: It’s a Real Shame the OnePlus 16 Is Launching Only in China
articles.content_orig:
OnePlus may be dead in most of the world , including the United States and Europe, but that doesn’t mean the company is done making interesting smartphones. In fact, quite the contrary: the OnePlus 16, just unveiled in China, looks pretty great.
The OnePlus 16 runs on Qualcomm’s latest flagship Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip. It has a 6.78-inch OLED screen, a huge 9,000 mAh battery, and some built-in lights that show a set of galactic coordinates, as The Verge notes . These lights also alert the user to incoming calls, messages, and other notifications. It’s not just neat but practically pointless space-related numbers.
The space theme also shows up in the phone’s colorways: Starlight, Martian Masterpiece, and Dark Forest, which admittedly has nothing to do with space.
The OnePlus 16’s overall design aesthetic carries forward quite a bit from last year’s OnePlus 15 , a somewhat disappointing end to OnePlus’ time as a global smartphone brand. After the excellent OnePlus 13 used Hasselblad-branded cameras to great effect , it was a shame to see the brand fall from grace with the OnePlus 15. It was fine, but felt like a step back in the camera department.
OnePlus hopes to right the ship a bit with the 16. It has a 200-megapixel main camera with a Type 1/1.4 image sensor and a 23mm equivalent f/1.6 lens. This is a big change from the OnePlus 15’s 50-megapixel main camera with a 24mm f/1.8 lens. The 15’s main camera featured a Type 1/1.56 sensor, by the way.
The 200MP primary camera is flanked by a 50-megapixel telephoto with a Type 1/1.95 sensor, 73mm equivalent lens, and f/2.6 aperture. There’s also a 50-megapixel 116° ultrawide camera with a relatively small Type 1/2.88 sensor.
While the ultrawide camera is unchanged, the telephoto looks like a step up. The lens is a bit shorter — 73mm versus 80mm equivalent — but it’s faster (f/2.6 versus f/2.8). The image sensor is also considerably larger. The OnePlus 15’s telephoto camera featured a Type 1/2.76 sensor.
Unfortunately, most of the world will not get to enjoy the OnePlus 16. For now, the device is launching exclusively in China, starting at 5,699 Chinese yuan, or around $850. OnePlus may have an exciting new smartphone on offer, but the company has still officially exited the North American and European markets.

articles.title_orig: Now 50 Years Old, One of the World’s Most Diverse Collection of Organisms Lives On at UT
articles.title_zh: Now 50 Years Old, One of the World’s Most Diverse Collection of Organisms Lives On at UT
articles.content_orig:
David Nobles Jr., curator of the UTEX Culture Collection of Algae, looks back and explains why algae matter in research.
All photos by Eileen Chong.
In 2026, a remarkable collection, unique to The University of Texas in Austin, celebrated its 50th anniversary –– the UTEX Culture Collection of Algae. David Nobles Jr., just the third curator of the collection in its 50 years, is charged with maintaining one of the most diverse collections of organisms anywhere on Earth.
Nobles is a world-class phycologist, the term he and his colleagues prefer for a person who studies algae (the other term, “algologist , ” also applies to people who study pain, and Nobles quipped that, though there can be days when that feels fitting, a distinction should be made). This summer, he and his colleagues moved their entire collection, more than 1,500 species, into a new space in the Moffett Molecular Biology Building at UT. We spoke with him to learn about the importance of the collection. This conversation has been edited for space.
Algae have been found to have tremendous commercial applications, from pharmaceuticals to fuel to mining. For example, phosphate is a limited resource vital to all agriculture, and algae are used to recover it from wastewater. Last year, we got a grant with a group from Sandia National Laboratories in Los Alamos to study algae that bind to rare earth elements. There are few accessible sources of such elements, which is why we call them rare, but these are critical minerals for our modern electronics, computers and phones. Some algae not only bind to these minerals naturally and efficiently, they can be made to collect the precious minerals in wastewater. So, we’ve been studying, including with an incredible group of undergraduates, which algae to use for bio-mining. It’s pretty amazing. Algae may give us an environmentally friendly way to mine rare earth metals.
What’s more, more than half of all carbon dioxide that’s naturally removed from our atmosphere is done so by algae. Algae are vital to our planet’s health. These organisms are also the bottom of the food chain in the oceans. Without them, there would be no marine life. They are often used to feed farm animals, so they are a primary source of protein and nutrients for us, too (plus, pretty much any time you buy a green smoothie to be healthy, one of its main ingredients is spirulina, a kind of algae). Of course, algae also frequently disrupt our lives, such as the frequent cyanobacterial blooms in lakes when no one can swim. For all these reasons, understanding algae better is critical.
Well, I like to tell people that algae is plural. That’s a good place to start because there is no singular group of organisms we can call alga.
Have you ever seen the tree of life? There are a few big domains like the eukaryotes, bacteria and archaea. Humans are on a single branch, near the bottom with all the other animals, under the eukaryotes. Plants are in another group of eukaryotes nearby. That means, even the most amazing zoo in the world focuses on organisms from only one group, the animals. The lushest botanical garden anywhere focuses on organisms from only one group, the plants. But what we call algae are not a single natural group. They are on many branches. So, we have 3,000 organisms from across the tree of life that we call algae. That’s why I always say our collection is perhaps the most diverse collection of living organisms in the world.
What we call algae are different organisms that share one characteristic. Most are a single cell, but they all use chlorophyll-a to gather energy from the sun through photosynthesis. And though they are green, they can be distinguished from plants because algae don’t have structures like roots, stems and leaves. Even so, plants stem from one group of algae in the tree of life, so one of my colleagues jokingly refers to plants as “higher and drier algae.” I like that.
Richard Starr, the founder of our collection, met a man named Ernst Pringsheim in 1953, who gifted him some cultures when they were both at Cambridge University in England. Pringsheim was one of the first people to study and grow algae in the early 1900s, and he escaped from the Nazis with his collection of about 400 strains several years before meeting Starr. Starr brought cultures back to the United States and grew the cultures into a collection, eventually returning to where he had gotten his Ph.D., here at UT. When he returned in 1976, he brought 2,000 strains with him, taking over a space in the Biological Laboratories Building and renamed it the UTEX Culture Collection. He was the director until he passed away unexpectedly in 1998, when Jerry Brand succeeded him. The collection still exists today largely because of Brand’s dedication and skill. We still have some of the original strains from the early 1900s in the collection because of him. Jerry retired in 2015, and I became just the third director. This year, the collection’s 50th anniversary, we finally moved out of our old space and into a new one in the Moffett Molecular Biology Building, a more modern space for the collection.
Mostly, the collection grew by accretion. Many researchers have private collections. After they retire, they will bequeath us their most important organisms, to take care of and make available to others. It’s a big responsibility, taking care of someone else’s life’s work. But it’s also a tremendous honor to do this for the community. I’ve just done my best to be a good steward of the collection.
We have the algae used in the original experiments that revealed the Calvin cycle. That’s the process in which carbon is removed from the air by photosynthetic organisms to make sugars, which not only helps the organisms grow but also provides food for all living creatures on Earth. Most people learn about it in school.
It’s a very hands-on job, taking care of 3,000 strains of living organisms. Jerry Brand, our former director, grew up on a farm, and he said the work was basically the same: Cows have to be milked every day; algae have to be tended to. That means we don’t get much time off. Most of our work is making food, what we call media, to grow the cultures. Algae can be pretty picky about what they consume. That’s OK because we don’t want them to be too happy and grow too quickly or they’d overwhelm the lab, so we are careful about what we feed them.
We spend much of our remaining time transferring the cultures and making new ones, which is a bit like making sourdough bread from a starter. We have to make sure the cultures don’t get contaminated when we grow new ones from old ones. We’re also a commercial enterprise. We distribute algae to researchers and companies around the world. We fulfill some 3,000 orders to every state in the United States and to some 50 or so countries every year. And more than 1,000 publications a year cite us.
In between, we make time to do research ourselves and train undergraduates. We’ve been lucky that almost half the collection is now frozen and preserved in liquid nitrogen, so we don’t have to care for all the strains we have every day.
So many algae do incredible, weird things. But it is probably Acetabularia , which people call maiden’s wineglass. It looks like a flower. It has a stem and a cup on the end, and it grows to be 7 or 8 centimeters long. But it is still just a single cell. They were very popular for many years in research because you can remove the base where the nucleus is and the cap will live on, because of its incredible messenger RNA. There’s another one I like called Valonia ventricosa , resembling a ping pong ball. They have a very thick cell wall on the outside, but the organism itself is just a thin sphere of protoplasm surrounding an empty space filled with air. When you pop one, all the cytoplasm very quickly makes tiny spheres. After a day or so, all those tiny spheres are new organisms. We show this all the time in demonstrations for the public.

articles.title_orig: Middaugh wins world title at XTERRA championships in New Mexico
articles.title_zh: Middaugh wins world title at XTERRA championships in New Mexico
articles.content_orig:
Two-time XTERRA short-track world champion Sullivan Middaugh earned his first full-distance world title at XTERRA’s 30th World Championship over the weekend in Ruidoso, New Mexico.
Middaugh, of EagleVail, won in 2:06:50, finishing five minutes and 56 seconds ahead of Spain’s Nacho Gálvez. Denmark’s Jens Emil Sloth Nielsen took third.
At Grindstone Lake, the water temperature was 64.6°F (18.1°C), while the air temperature was 53.2°F (11.8°C) an hour before the start. At Wingfield Park, morning temperatures were around 59°F (15°C), with a high near 70°F (21°C).
The course began with a 1.5K swim before climbing into rocky singletrack on a single 27K mountain-bike lap. Riders crossed the high terrain around Grindstone Mesa before descending toward the village. The final 10K run took athletes through village streets and forest trails, returning through Wingfield Park between the two laps and into the finish.
Gálvez led out of Grindstone Lake in 18:21, followed closely by Sullivan and Porter Middaugh. Sullivan felt comfortable in the water and wanted to reach the singletrack first, knowing Sloth Nielsen would be chasing from behind.
Both leaders described falls early on the bike. Gálvez crashed on the first corner, while Middaugh fell on the third and lost his bike computer.
“I think it was maybe a blessing in disguise not to have power data,” Middaugh said. “I just rode how I was feeling and rode as hard as I could the whole time.”
His 1:07:18 bike split was the fastest in the elite men’s field. He carried his advantage into the run and added another leading split of 39:00.
“I knew that at altitude I could run uphill just as fast as anyone else,” he said. “So I pushed every climb, let it roll on every descent, and just gave it everything I could.”
Gálvez kept chasing after his fall and held second through the run. “But I never lost faith,” he said. “On the run, I gave everything I had, and I was able to finish second. I’m super happy.”
Sloth Nielsen worked forward from 13th at bike start to complete the podium, crediting the preparation of the two athletes ahead of him. “Sullivan and Nacho must have just prepared better,” he said. “They’ve been at altitude for longer.”
Arthur Serrières finished fourth, followed by Maxim Chané. Josiah Middaugh placed sixth and Porter seventh, putting all three Middaughs inside the top ten.
“Just a proud day,” Josiah said. “Really happy for Sullivan. Start to finish, he just put it together.”
Porter finished after a heavy bike crash and described racing alongside his father as both inspiring and helpful in getting him through the course.
XTERRA had been part of childhood for the Middaugh brothers before it became a championship ambition.
“It means everything. It’s how we grew up, watching our dad and going to races with him,” Sullivan said.
He also remembered Arthur Serrières encouraging him after his first Worlds in Maui in 2021. “I remember Arthur telling me at the dinner afterwards to stick with it,” he said. “At that point, he was already a world champion, so that meant a lot.”

articles.title_orig: RIT student’s designs will help power world’s first Electron-Ion Collider
articles.title_zh: RIT student’s designs will help power world’s first Electron-Ion Collider
articles.content_orig:
Scott Hamilton/ RIT Photography
RIT student Robert Desjardins designed the four-tiered storage system to hold the superconducting magnets that will be installed in the new Electron-Ion Collider at Brookhaven Laboratory.
When the U.S. Department of Energy’s Brookhaven National Laboratory needed multiple stands that could each support up to 45,000 pounds of superconducting magnets in limited space, a Rochester Institute of Technology student designed the solution.
Fourth-year mechanical engineering technology student Robert Desjardins spent his summer internship redesigning storage stands that will help Brookhaven prepare for the world's first Electron-Ion Collider (EIC), a next-generation particle accelerator that will help scientists understand the building blocks of matter.
During his 10-week internship, Desjardins developed a four-level design capable of safely storing 20-foot-long magnets weighing more than 10,000 pounds each. The stands will allow magnets being removed from the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC), in service for more than 26 years at Brookhaven, to be stored for reuse on the new Electron-Ion Collider, which is expected to become operational in the mid-2030s.
“The original stands were designed in the 1990s, and at the time they could hold only three of the magnets. They wanted to up the capacity to four,” said Desjardins. “I had to get my project fully designed, look at blueprints, revise computer-aided models, and start talking to the manufacturers and simulate some of the strength tests required.”
RIT alumnus and Brookhaven mechanical engineer Jonathon Greene '15 ( mechanical engineering ), who helped oversee the project, served as Desjardins’s mentor during the internship.
David Rahner/Brookhaven National Laboratory
RIT alumnus Jonathon Greene, right, and Desjardins are pictured in front of the new four-tier magnet storage stand Desjardins designed. Greene, who has been at Brookhaven National Laboratory since 2022, mentored Desjardins through his internship. They are standing next to a superconducting magnet.
In an article written by the lab, Greene credits Desjardins’s work with significant project savings. “Rob costed down the original design while increasing the height. We saved about $420,000 by doing so.”
Greene said he expects about 80 magnets will come out of RHIC and need to be stored for the EIC using Desjardins’s design.
During the prototype development, Desjardins met regularly with Greene and presented status information to the larger group of project engineers and scientists, fielding tough questions about materials, status of safety reviews, and results of simulations testing for load capacity and even seismic analysis.
“In engineering you have to simulate for the worst at all times. I did so many simulations; the design was half the project. The other half was performing the simulations and checking my work,” said Desjardins, who is from West Sayville, N.Y., and is also working on a master’s degree in mechatronics and mechanical systems in RIT’s College of Engineering Technology .
Both Greene and Desjardins attribute some success in the field to participating on co-ops and internships that provide students with real-world experience. Technical coursework in 3D modeling, strength of materials, and load tolerance are foundational concepts for engineers. These were the skills Desjardins said he learned at RIT and brought to the Brookhaven project.
RIT’s renowned internship and co-op program , one of the oldest and largest in the nation, allows students to learn on the job and define their career paths. More than 4,000 RIT students completed co-ops or internships last year, engaging in paid work experience at national and global companies and organizations in nearly every industry.
“This was such a great experience, to learn and hear feedback on a project from experienced engineers, experts at their craft, and to be part of such a huge international project,” said Desjardins. “This was all real teamwork and it was great.”

articles.title_orig: More damage expected in Long Beach after powerful surf from Tropical Storm Rachel hammers coast
articles.title_zh: More damage expected in Long Beach after powerful surf from Tropical Storm Rachel hammers coast
articles.content_orig:
Inspectors are assessing damaged homes between Long Beach high tides.
LONG BEACH, Calif. (KABC) -- Destructive waves from the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel continued crashing into homes on the Long Beach Peninsula for a fourth day, leaving several properties on the verge of ruin and inspectors with limited time to assess the damage before the next high tide.
Eight buildings along the boardwalk have been red-tagged so far, affecting 13 individual addresses, while one building has been yellow-tagged. The number could change as inspectors get a closer look at the damage.
Crews had a small window of daylight between Sunday night’s high tide and another high tide around 10 a.m. Monday to inspect the homes and determine whether additional buildings needed to be tagged. They will have another brief window before Monday night’s high tide.
In an update on Monday afternoon, Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson said no additional homes were tagged after Monday morning's high tide.
“We’re not out of the woods yet,” Richardson said.
He said crews continue to build sand berms and fortify areas near the damaged boardwalk. Vehicle access continues to be limited to residents only on the peninsula.
Richardson noted that a three-month project to rebuild the beach and bring in more sand begins next week.
Video from AIR7 shows worsening damage from the relentless waves, including cracked walls of several homes and smashed windows and doors. The destruction extends beyond the exteriors of the homes, with waves washing away sand from beneath the buildings and potentially shifting their foundations.
One home had a crack stretching from its foundation to the roof, and the front half of the building appeared to have shifted.
“As the waves are hitting these structures, it's pulling the soil away from the foundations and the substructures of these buildings, potentially undermining the foundations of these buildings,” said Dan Fox, president of the Structural Engineers Association of Southern California.
A mandatory evacuation order remains in place for residents on 64th and 65th streets along Seaside Walk.
“Long Beach is on sand, right? We’re built on sand. If the ocean gets far enough into the structures where the sand sits, it sucks it out. This is what happens,” Long Beach resident Gabriella Holt said. “I’ve lived here 12 years and have never seen anything... even just this collapse.”
Some of the sand berms built along the beach in an effort to protect homes have completely washed away.
Neighbors told Eyewitness News that although they place sandbags and prepare for high surf and flooding each year, they were not mentally prepared for this level of destruction.
"It's unbelievable because, here in Long Beach, you think that you're safe from big huge waves and things because of the break wall," said resident Monica Delrosario. "When you see the force of just a swell bringing those waves and doing the destruction that they're doing, it makes you realize that you just never know with Mother Nature."

articles.title_orig: Trump defends Russia diesel deal after bipartisan pushback: 'I made the right choice'
articles.title_zh: Trump defends Russia diesel deal after bipartisan pushback: 'I made the right choice'
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Monday defended last week's decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel fuel exports after the announcement drew bipartisan criticism .
Trump, in a Truth Social post , accused the media of hypocrisy for allegedly refusing to cover past purchases of Russian energy by the European Union.
"The European Union paid Russia 250 Billion Dollars for Energy, and the Fake News Media doesn't want to get near that story," Trump wrote.
While the president did not specify, his figure roughly tracks with some estimates of how much the EU has spent importing fossil fuels from Russia since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The European Commission has launched a plan to phase out its dependence on Russian energy.
"I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!" Trump wrote in the social media post.
Lawmakers from both parties raised concerns about Trump's decision to let Russia supply some diesel to the U.S. and global markets for the next six months.
The plan received pushback from multiple congressional Republicans who have urged Trump not to lift the U.S. ban on energy imports from Russia until its president, Vladimir Putin , ends the war against Ukraine.
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," a group of seven senators, including four Republicans, said in a joint statement on Sunday.
Other Republicans have also raised issues with Trump's deal.
"While I understand the desire to bring down diesel prices, I am concerned the lifting of sanctions on Russian oil will only fund the Kremlin's war machine—emboldening more violence and destruction, as we have seen in recent days," Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas, said Friday.
Trump, whose party is staring down a potentially tough midterm election that has coincided with widespread economic dissatisfaction, says the plan he coordinated with Putin will help bring down sky-high diesel prices. Some analysts say the policy won't make much of a dent , however.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that the U.S. easing sanctions on Moscow "plays into Russia's hands."

articles.content_orig:
Published Oct 12, 2026 at 11:00 a.m. ET
Published Oct 12, 2026 at 11:00 a.m. ET

Gothamist is funded by sponsors and member donations
Gov. Kathy Hochul has declared a disaster emergency in response to the spread of measles across rural parts of New York state and neighboring Pennsylvania.
But what exactly does that mean?
Dr. James McDonald, the state health commissioner, discussed the disaster declaration and what’s driving it, with All Things Considered host Sean Carlson.
Here’s a transcript of their conversation, edited for length and clarity:
What it means right now is we now have additional authority granted to us by the governor. We have 110 cases of measles so far in New York state. That's more than twice what we had all of last year. The executive order gives us new tools. One tool is, more healthcare workers can administer the vaccine: EMTs, paramedics, pharmacists, community midwives, all trusted people in the community. That helps us.
Another tool we have in the executive order is, we can have more testing done, so nurses can do standing orders and have testing for measles. That helps us find cases quicker, and that will help us identify more cases of measles. The third thing it does is, we get immunization information on adults in our data registry so we know what communities have had the vaccine. That'll help us better plan for where we're likely to see more outbreaks.
It’s rural New York, and really what we're seeing is, there's a lot of local spread in rural New York.
Now, keep in mind, what I mean by that is, it's the most contagious disease out there. So what you see is people come home, and then they spread it to their family, and it spreads really quickly. If your family's not immunized, you're almost all going to get infected. When I say it's the most contagious disease, it doesn't have to be this way. Measles is preventable, almost 100% preventable.
The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine — the one that's been around since 1971 — it's the only way to prevent measles, and it really is our best tool in the toolbox. We have to get more people immunized as quickly as possible, so we can really achieve community immunity. We need to get back to that.
One of the things I wanted to underscore nationally is, what's been going on the last two years in the United States is not normal. When you look at the data for 2025, we had almost 2,400 cases of measles in the United States. This year we have almost 3,700 cases and climbing. This is not normal.
What you've been seeing for the prior 25 years was we would average under 100 cases a year, and I don't want us to be desensitized to that. We should not be tolerating thousands of cases as a country every year of a vaccine-preventable disease.
One of the things about measles, it starts out looking like a cough, runny nose, your eyes get watery, maybe a little bit red, and then you get the rash a few days into it, and you might get spots inside your throat. Where it gets really serious is when people get pneumonia. People do end up with respiratory failure. They can end up on breathing machines. About 1 in 5 people we know about with measles are ending up in a hospital.
It is not a mild childhood illness. It is a serious disease. And one of the things that's unusual about the outbreak we're seeing right now is, two out of three cases are in adults.
And one of the things that's important to remember is New York has really good vaccine requirements , but they're school-entry requirements, so if you're an adult between 18 and 69, you really need to have made sure you've had two measles, mumps and rubella vaccines in your life. If you don't know that, contact your local health department or your doctor's office and get a measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. It's just that simple.
If you haven't had two measles, mumps and rubella vaccines, you need to be concerned because the vaccine doesn't respect borders. One of the things about measles people need to remember is, people are very contagious four days before they start having symptoms. So they don't even know they're going to have measles, but that's when they're very contagious, and they're contagious four days after their symptoms start, which can be kind of mild.
And this is really the main point: You can't tell that you're being exposed all the time.
Western New York, Central New York, and Northern New York really are the areas I'm most concerned about, and I think it's important to understand that we really don't have great data on adult immunization rates.
The way New York state law is constructed, we know about everyone under 18 who's got an immunization. We don't know about adults. One of the things the executive order gives me, though, is now I'll be able to at least know which adults are getting the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine. That will help me. And we have had some success.
You know, it's not always vaccine-hesitant communities. Sometimes there's vaccine-unaware communities. We've administered over 1,200 measles, mumps, and rubella vaccines. What we're finding, though, is after a long conversation, and often it's kitchen-table public health. What I mean by that is local health departments literally going into someone's home, immunizing right at the kitchen table, and if that's where people want to be met, we're all for it. We're happy to meet people where they are, very happy with the way local health departments are literally knocking on doors, offering the vaccine, and answering questions.

Google’s Fitbit lineup expanded on Monday with the introduction of the Fitbit Edge, a new wearable that’s positioned between the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch.
Priced at $179.99, it combines the Fitbit Air’s slim band with an OLED display for checking map directions, notifications, weather, and music controls.
Like the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air, the Edge works with Google Health Coach, powered by Gemini. (You’ll need a Google Health Premium subscription to use it.) The coach can use your fitness, health, and medical information to put together weekly routines and workout plans, then adjust them around your schedule.
It also comes with Google’s Health Guardian feature, which is designed to spot notable changes in health measurements over time, including indicators related to blood pressure and insulin resistance. (The company announced these features at the Pixel Watch 5 launch in August.)
Google says the Fitbit Edge can automatically recognize and log up to 100 activities, including runs, bike rides, and walks. The company explains it uses context from your movement to work out what you’re doing and add it to your weekly goals. Plus, the device supports more than 50 exercise modes and can offer on-screen prompts during workouts, such as a nudge to push harder or take a breather.
The Fitbit Edge’s built-in GPS is 40% more accurate than the previous generation, the company claims, which should make it easier to track outdoor runs. Google says sleep-stage detection is also 15% more accurate than on earlier generations, helping the device provide better sleep summaries and coaching tips.
Meanwhile, the battery is rated for up to seven days on a charge, and the wearable is water-resistant to 50 meters.
The Fitbit Edge is available to preorder through the Google Store, with store availability set for October 27.
Color choices include Obsidian, Fog, Olive, and Canyon. There’s also a Stephen Curry Special Edition, priced at $219.99.

A St. Louis Park, Minnesota, woman broke a Guinness World Record Sunday for rucking a half marathon while carrying a 40 pound pack.
Megan Corey ran the half marathon in two hours and three minutes. The previous record was two hours and 20 minutes. Corey also beat the record for the 20 pound ruck during the same race in Dundas.
"First time going for a Guinness World Record," said Corey. "I found out about the Guinness World Record for the fastest half marathon for females carrying a pack when I did a half marathon in Tennessee last year and it was a 20 pound pack half marathon. And found out after from a fellow racer that I had broken the 20 pound record, unbeknownst to me. But you have to predeclare. So today I'm predeclaring and going for the 40 pound record."
The previous 20 pound record was two hours and 34 minutes.

articles.title_orig: GROHE Announces Winner of 2026 GROHE Water Prize at the World Architecture Festival
articles.title_zh: GROHE Announces Winner of 2026 GROHE Water Prize at the World Architecture Festival
articles.content_orig:
The award-winning, "Terracotta Fog Water Harvester" addresses an innovative terracotta facade tile system to harvest atmospheric fog.
FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. , Oct. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- GROHE , a global leader in bathroom solutions and kitchen fittings, has announced the winner of the 2026 GROHE Water Prize for the World Architecture Festival (WAF), slated to be held this year from November 18–20 in Fort Lauderdale.
A Carnegie Mellon University School of Architecture team, spearheaded by Associate Professor and Lead Researcher, Laura Garófalo, has been awarded the £10,000 prize for " Bio-inspired Architectural Terracotta for Sustainable Water Harvesting ," an initiative designed to advance community water self-sufficiency in arid, fog-prone regions. Combining ancient ceramic craftsmanship with digital fabrication and surface physics, the project uses modular terracotta tiles for fog water-harvesting. Drawing design inspiration from leaf venation and the Namib Desert beetle, the tiles pair hydrophilic (water-attracting) clay peaks with hydrophobic (water-repelling) glazed channels to capture fog up to 400% more efficiently than standard flat surfaces.
As a rigid, mineral-based alternative to traditional synthetic plastic netting, the terracotta concept eliminates microplastic pollution while offering a significantly smaller carbon footprint. Designed for future integration into building facades and rainscreen systems, the research shows how exterior walls could one day act as durable, decentralized freshwater collection systems that strengthen local health and climate resilience.
Of the winning project, Patrick Speck, Leader, LIXIL Global Design, Europe & Americas and a jury member of the GROHE Water Prize, remarked: "At GROHE, we believe the future of water stewardship requires rethinking how our built environment interacts with natural resources. By transforming a building facade into an active water-harvesting asset, this project embodies GROHE's design ethos, in which biomimicry, material craft, and human-centered purpose converge to reshape how society experiences water."
"Receiving the Grohe Water Prize is an honor critical to advancing the development of our bio-inspired architectural terracotta system," said Laura Garófolo, Associate Professor at Carnegie Mellon University. "It will make it possible to move through material experimentation toward a scalable architectural application for sustainable water harvesting. We are deeply grateful to GROHE for recognizing the potential of design and architecture to address the growing challenges surrounding water."
Paul Finch, Programme Director, World Architecture Festival, and fellow jury member, added, "As ever, reviewing this year's entries was a pleasure, and we congratulate GROHE for continuing to support this research prize. This year's standout winner offers a brilliant approach to harvesting atmospheric fog - research with clear potential to benefit numerous regions around the world. It is particularly fitting that such an idea should emerge as WAF explores the theme of 'Water' at this year's festival in Fort Lauderdale. We look forward to the project presentation on Thursday, 19 November on the Festival Hall Stage."
With over 50 entries for this year's prize, each submission examined the evolving relationship between water, architecture, and community through innovative, future-focused design. The shortlisted projects demonstrated a remarkable breadth of ideas. Among this year's standout finalists were:
Projecto Vito Volcanic Catchment: An off-grid marine conservation headquarters on Fogo Island featuring vaulted brick roofscapes that serve as the primary rainwater and fog-harvesting system in a region without surface freshwater. Project submitted by Studio Ma (Applicant) with Associação Projecto Vitó — NGO co-applicant (Lead researcher: Christiana Moss, FAIA)
Glasgow Bath Commons: An adaptive reuse project transforming an abandoned railway viaduct and church into a civic water commons that integrates rainwater harvesting, heat recovery, and public bathing culture. Project submitted by Lap Shing Sy.
Lo—TEK Water: A Field Guide for TEKnology: Applied research supporting the Miccosukee–ReefLine Biocultural Stewardship Corridor of Miami Beach, integrating underwater public reef infrastructure with Indigenous co-governance frameworks. Project submitted by Julia Watson
Since 2017, the GROHE Water Prize has supported innovative projects addressing global water challenges, underscoring the transformative potential of water-conscious design for the built environment. While also reflecting the values at the heart of GROHE: combining sustainable innovation, exceptional design, advanced technology, and enduring quality to elevate everyday experiences and help protect one of our planet's most precious resources.
About GROHE GROHE is a leading global brand for complete bathroom solutions and kitchen fittings. Since 2014, GROHE has been a cornerstone of LIXIL's global portfolio of pioneering water and housing brands. To deliver "Pure Freude an Wasser", every product is based on the brand pillars of quality, technology, design and sustainability. From curated experiences within our luxury sub-brand GROHE SPA to refined water solutions for every home, we provide products tailored to the exacting requirements of our professional partners and their differentiated target groups.
With water at the core of everything we do, we manage our value chain and its impact responsibly, contributing to LIXIL's Impact Strategy . By developing technologies that optimize water- and energy-saving potential, we empower a more conscious use of resources without ever compromising on "Pure Freude an Wasser".
About LIXIL LIXIL (TSE Code 5938) makes pioneering water and housing products that solve everyday, real-life challenges, making better homes a reality for everyone, everywhere. Drawing on our Japanese heritage, we create world-leading technology and innovate to make high quality products that transform homes. But the LIXIL difference is how we do this; through meaningful design, an entrepreneurial spirit, a dedication to improving accessibility for all, and responsible business growth. Our approach comes to life through industry leading brands, including INAX, GROHE, American Standard, and TOSTEM. Approximately 53,000 colleagues operating in more than 150 countries are proud to make products that touch the lives of more than a billion people every day. Learn more at www.lixil.com

articles.title_orig: 2 American economists win Nobel for work on managing economic shocks
articles.title_zh: 2 American economists win Nobel for work on managing economic shocks
articles.content_orig:
English English (pdf) Swedish Swedish (pdf)
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has decided to award the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2026 to
Robert E. Hall Stanford University, CA, USA.
Michael Woodford Columbia University, New York, USA.
“for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”
This year’s laureates in the economic sciences, Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford, have developed new macroeconomic models that have significantly improved our ability to implement effective stabilisation policy. On the basis of these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the economy’s peaks and troughs.
The economy is characterised by alternating downturns and upturns. Ever since the economist John Maynard Keynes launched his theories almost a century ago, stabilisation policy has been important for tackling these fluctuations. During recessions, the economy is boosted by reducing interest rates and increasing the budget deficit, while the opposite should be done to slow a booming economy.
However, during the oil crises of the 1970s, it seemed that the Keynesian models that govern when and how measures should be implemented no longer worked. They did not reduce unemployment, but led to uncontrolled inflation instead. The West experienced a decade of low growth, high unemployment and high inflation. Many people believed that stabilisation policy had done more harm than good and that it should be retired.
Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford are awarded this year’s prize in economic sciences for demonstrating how economic models could be reconstructed to revitalise stabilisation policy. Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation. This encompasses an understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions.
A central component in these models is that households and businesses are forward looking when making decisions about savings or product prices. When governments and central banks communicate their plans for economic policy, they can influence this view of the future and move the economy in the right direction. Since the new models’ introduction, they have been extremely helpful in dealing with the economic downturns that have affected us.
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” says John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.

articles.title_orig: Apple has reportedly increased its iPhone Duo orders by 30%

articles.content_orig:
A new report by Securities Times in China indicates Apple is now anticipating much higher demand for iPhone Duo than initially expected, despite pre-orders not starting until later this week.
Apple launches iPhone Duo pre-orders this Friday, October 16. And you’ll be able to start your pre-order process for the fastest checkout later today .
But despite pre-orders not being live yet, Apple seems to be anticipating significantly higher demand for iPhone Duo than its initial estimates.
According to a report from China’s Securities Times , Apple has increased its orders for iPhone Duo in the supply chain by a massive 30%.
The report says total supply for the remainder of 2026 still doesn’t exceed 10 million units. But based on prior estimates of 6-7 million units being produced, it’s likely that the new target number is close to 10 million.
Clearly, Apple is seeing a better than expected response to the iPhone Duo since its unveiling last month. And its planned retail push adds more evidence to support that.
Supply chain sources also tell Securities Times that iPhone 18 Pro Max orders have increased by 10-15% and iPhone 18 Pro orders have been reduced by 10-15%. The total supply targets for the iPhone 18 Pro line overall are ultimately unchanged, however, contradicting a recent Nikkei Asia report .

articles.title_orig: World War II notes linked to ‘The Great Escape’ prison camp found in garage crawlspace
articles.title_zh: World War II notes linked to ‘The Great Escape’ prison camp found in garage crawlspace
articles.content_orig:
A man in upstate New York discovered more than cobwebs and missing holiday decorations while recently cleaning out his garage. Behind a small wood plank, homeowner Jason Hurdle spotted a long-forgotten crawlspace stuffed with vintage milk pails, a safe, and a dusty box of files . Hurdle intended to simply toss the papers in the trash, until a perfectly timed gust of wind removed the crate’s lid. Only then did he realize the box’s true contents: dozens of reports labeled “Secret” relating to Stalag Luft 3, an infamous prison camp run by the Nazi Luftwaffe near Germany’s western border during World War II . Over 300 pages of handwritten accounts from U.S. soldiers recounting their brutal incarcerations at the facility under conditions “not fit for humans.”
“I feel the hurt, the pain, and a lot of things these guys have been through,” Hurdle recently told local news outlet WHEC .
A visit from specialists at the National Archives quickly confirmed the authenticity of the questionnaires, which were compiled in 1945 following Allied liberations of German POW camps. The box was clearly intended for use as evidence of war crimes, which the reports corroborate in tragic detail. Soldiers wrote about living in facilities with “no heat, no beds” while exposed to the elements and vermin. Other troops recalled grueling work on rail lines while witnessing beatings, executions, and even the “cold blooded murder” of surrendering armed forces. Stalag Luft 3 is famously the site of a breakout later recounted by former prisoner Paul Brickhill in the book and 1963 film adaptation, The Great Escape .
“When I first laid them on the table in front of them, the first thing the one agent said was, ‘These are original, we want these,’” added Hurdle.
It’s still unclear how the box ended up inside the garage crawlspace. Hurdle suspects they may have belonged to a retired U.S. Army officer who once lived next door, especially since the box also contained other personal items from the man’s family. In any case, the indispensable historical accounts are now under the care of the National Archives, who have since digitized and unclassified the reports. The entirety of the discovery is now available online to the public.
